records.title: Towards Engineering Multi-Agent LLMs: A Protocol-Driven Approach

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Comparative evidence that explicit contracts, typed messaging, and verification-gated lifecycle control can improve one multi-agent system relative to another. It does not compare multi-agent operation with a single agent and therefore supports complementary production-hardening methods more strongly than the focal single-versus-multi hypothesis.
evidence_notes.research_design: Preliminary evaluation of SEMAP against a MetaGPT baseline on HumanEval function development, ProgramDev deployment-level development, devign100 C/C++ vulnerability detection, and vudenc100 Python vulnerability detection. Development uses a centralized five-role setup and up to five collaboration rounds; vulnerability detection uses decentralized Auditor, Critic, and Tester agents for one round. Both DeepSeek-V3-0324 and gpt-4.1-nano-2025-04-14 are tested. A separate gpt-4o-2024-08-06 judge applies the MAST failure taxonomy for under-specification, inter-agent misalignment, and verification failure.

held_constant: The same two underlying model versions and task datasets are used across baseline and SEMAP conditions.
Both conditions use the same maximum of five rounds for development and one round for vulnerability detection.
Both vulnerability-detection conditions use the same three decentralized roles.
omitted_or_confounded: The baseline is implemented in MetaGPT while SEMAP is middleware over Google's A2A infrastructure, so protocol effects are entangled with framework and implementation differences.
No single-agent LLM, domain detector, or non-agent protocol baseline is included.
The outcome is judge-classified failure count rather than functional task success, code quality, vulnerability-detection precision/recall, or production behavior.
No ablation isolates behavioral contracts, structured messaging, or lifecycle verification.
Resource overhead, token use, latency, and cost are not measured.
Artifacts were not yet released in the paper, limiting independent reproduction.

headline_results.finding: On HumanEval, total judged failures fall from 256 to 92 with GPT-4.1-nano (64.1%) and from 112 to 34 with DeepSeek-V3 (69.6%). Under-specification falls by 71.5% and 73.0%, respectively.

On ProgramDev, total failures fall from 103 to 90 with GPT-4.1-nano (12.6%) and from 67 to 29 with DeepSeek-V3 (56.7%). The wide model-dependent difference is negative evidence against assuming uniform protocol gains.
For vulnerability detection, total judged failures fall by 28.2% and 8.3% on devign100, and by 47.4% and 16.4% on vudenc100, for GPT-4.1-nano and DeepSeek-V3 respectively.
By round 5, HumanEval under-specification failures reach 2 for GPT-SEMAP and 0 for DeepSeek-SEMAP, versus 9 and 2 for their baselines; ProgramDev reaches 3 and 0, versus 3 and 3.
The authors infer that SEMAP produces more stable collaboration because baseline failures reappear after temporary drops. Component-level causality remains untested without ablation.

limitations: The experiment demonstrates protocol-versus-framework improvement, not specialized multi-agent superiority over a matched single agent.
Failure counts can assign more than one category per instance and do not directly reveal whether the final software or vulnerability label is correct.
Only two models, two development datasets, and two 100-sample vulnerability subsets are included.
The paper calls the evaluation preliminary and explicitly leaves larger datasets, longer workflows, more baselines, and ablations to future work.
future_work: Scale to larger datasets, more agents, and longer workflows.

records.title: From benchmarks to deployment: a comprehensive review of agentic AI evaluation

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Review-level evidence about why apparent agent gains often fail to establish production readiness. It does not empirically compare a specialized multi-agent system with a matched single agent, but it supplies an evaluation framework for making such comparisons credible and deployable.
evidence_notes.research_design: Systematic review following a stated PRISMA process over IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, arXiv, Google Scholar, and Springer for 2021-2025. The paper reports 1,247 initial records, 384 after deduplication and title/abstract screening, 95 after full-text review, then 89 eligible papers and 52 included papers: 15 primary benchmarks plus 37 supporting works. Fifteen benchmarks are compared across task structure, metrics, datasets, validity, reproducibility, and deployment gaps. Two authors independently scored five benchmarks across five rubric dimensions, agreeing exactly on 21/25 ratings (84%).

held_constant: The review applies a common deployment-gap vocabulary across 15 heterogeneous benchmarks.
Its rubric operationalizes cost transparency, safety coverage, maintainability, trajectory quality, and robustness on a common 0-5 scale.
A two-rater check covers five selected benchmarks and all five rubric dimensions.
omitted_or_confounded: No primary matched experiment compares single-agent and multi-agent architectures.
The benchmarks span incompatible domains and tasks; conclusions are comparative review judgments rather than a meta-analysis of common effect sizes.
Rubric reliability is checked on only 5 of 15 benchmarks, with disagreements resolved by discussion rather than an independently reported chance-corrected statistic.
The PRISMA narrative moves from 95 papers after full-text review to 89 eligible papers without explaining six exclusions.
The paper reports many deployment statistics from cited studies; these are secondary evidence and were not generated or independently replicated by this review.
Architecture-specific claims remain conceptual because the review does not stratify matched benchmark outcomes by single-agent versus multi-agent design.

headline_results.finding: Across the 15 reviewed benchmarks, security is absent in 15/15 primary evaluation schemes; cost is only partially represented by action counts in 2/15 and absent in 13/15; safety is partial in 1/15; robustness is partial in 3/15. The conclusion summarizes that 13/15 rely on binary success as the sole criterion and 14/15 do not measure trajectory quality.

The deployment-readiness rubric assigns SWE-bench 20% and WebArena approximately 45%; no reviewed benchmark exceeds 50%. These are author-designed rubric scores, not observed deployment success rates.

The review reports that test-pass rate and code quality correlate at r=0.31, and elsewhere reports a SWE-bench deployment sample with test-pass versus acceptance correlation r=0.43 and maintainability correlation r=0.12. These values are synthesized from cited sources rather than estimated in this review.

Outcome-only metrics cannot distinguish coherent planning from trial-and-error, efficient tool use from brute-force retries, or materially different failure modes in ReAct, Reflexion, and multi-agent architectures.

The authors argue that evaluation methodology, rather than model capability, is now the principal deployment bottleneck. The benchmark-gap counts support widespread measurement omissions, but the stronger causal formulation is a review thesis rather than an experimentally isolated result.

limitations: The review focuses on LLM-based agents; reinforcement-learning and neuro-symbolic agents are excluded.

Benchmark-selection thresholds are described differently across sections (at least 50 citations or major venue on page 11; more than 100 citations or major deployment for the 15 representatives on page 14).
The common rubric imposes expert judgments on heterogeneous domains, and only a subset receives duplicate ratings.
Several exact production claims depend on supporting citations and should not be treated as primary data from this paper.
Data availability states that no datasets were generated or analyzed, even though benchmark attributes and rubric scores are presented; no separate extraction dataset is described.

Use continuous lifecycle evaluation and versioned dynamic tasks to detect regressions and distribution drift.

Test transfer across task families, environments, and functionally equivalent toolsets.

combinable_methods: Trajectory-level scoring of planning coherence, tool selection, retries, and error recovery.

Safety-constrained scoring, adversarial cases, and runtime contract monitoring for silent failures.

quotes.use: Core review evidence for systematic deployment-metric omissions.

quotes.text: This is problematic in the case of architecture different agents where ReAct systems, Reflexion frameworks, and multi-agent architectures have different trajectory structures, which are not well represented by existing metrics.

records.title: An LLM-based multi-agent framework for agile effort estimation

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Adjacent evidence for human-agent consensus and role-specialized discussion, but not evidence that a multi-agent system outperforms a matched single agent. evidence_notes.research_design: Two-part evaluation. RQ1 tests a standalone SEEAgent long-term-memory component using base and project-specific QLoRA-fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct against Deep-SE, GPT2SP, and Fine-SE on four public Jira projects (DM, ME, TD, US; 4,907 total issues), preserving Fine-SE train/test splits and using MAE, MMRE, PRED(50), Wilcoxon tests, and Vargha-Delaney effect sizes. RQ2 is a human study with 12 purposively recruited practitioners. Each session uses three human developers, two GPT-4o-mini SEEAgents with front-end or back-end role prompts, and the first author as product owner on a simplified 33-story e-commerce project, followed by a 12-item Likert and two-question open survey.

held_constant: RQ1 uses the same datasets, train/test splits, and metrics as prior effort-estimation baselines, and baseline code is replicated.
Base and fine-tuned SEEAgent variants share Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; fine-tuning is performed separately per project.

RQ2 has no human-only, one-agent, non-specialized-agent, or alternative-model control condition, and it reports perceptions rather than estimation accuracy or convergence quality.

The human study uses GPT-4o-mini and in-context examples, whereas RQ1 uses fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B; the two evaluations do not validate the same configuration.
No token, cost, latency, number-of-rounds-to-consensus, or convergence-failure metric is reported.

headline_results.finding: The fine-tuned standalone SEEAgent is best across all three metrics on DM, ME, and US, but not TD. On ME it records MAE 1.217, MMRE 0.414, and PRED(50) 0.747; on US it records 0.350, 0.085, and 1.000.

The human sample is 12 participants on one simplified project, limiting industrial and cross-domain generalization.
The paper describes the human study as rigorous, but the design measures post-session sentiment without a comparator or behavioral ground truth.
The RQ1 projects are highly imbalanced in size; TD has only 73 records and produces the negative result.

Add voice interaction while preserving auditable communication traces.

records.title: Evaluation of the Choice of LLM in a Multi-Agent Solution for GUI-Test Generation

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Negative and boundary evidence about specialization inside a multi-agent architecture. The experiment compares heterogeneous model constellations with homogeneous model constellations across specialized roles; its phrase 'single LLM across all agents' means one model type reused by multiple agents, not a single-agent system.
evidence_notes.research_design: PathFinder assigns perception/summarization, decision-making, data extraction, and validation to four agents. Mistral-Nemo, Gemma2, and Llama3.1 (4-bit local quantizations) are exhaustively permuted across the first three roles; Gemma2 is fixed as Oracle. All 27 constellations run 10 times on each of four e-commerce sites for one purchase task, totaling 1,080 runs. Temperature is 0.1, Perceptron context is 8K, other contexts are 4K, and execution is capped at 31 steps. One experimenter manually classifies all runs, with ambiguous cases discussed among authors. Outcomes are F1, median steps, and median duration.

held_constant: All 27 assignments of the same three models to the three varied roles are tested on the same task and four sites with ten repeated runs.
Agent architecture, role definitions, local hardware, generation temperature, step cap, and fixed Oracle model are shared across constellations.
Using every permutation permits direct homogeneous-versus-heterogeneous comparisons within PathFinder.
omitted_or_confounded: There is no single-agent architecture baseline, so the experiment cannot estimate the benefit of role decomposition itself.
Gemma2 is fixed as Oracle after pilots because other models terminated early, which removes one role from the factorial comparison and embeds a development-informed choice.
The same prompts are reused across models, but the authors observe model-specific prompt failures and acknowledge prompt bias.
Only one task, four sites, three similarly sized quantized local models, one machine, and one primary human evaluator are included.
The paper reports descriptive F1 differences but no confidence intervals or inferential test for homogeneous versus heterogeneous constellations.

F1 treats the Oracle's success/failure judgment as classification, while true-negative versus false-negative assignment partly depends on expert judgment about whether a timed-out task was theoretically completable.

headline_results.finding: For individual fixed websites, a homogeneous constellation is among the best: Gemma2/Gemma2/Gemma2 reaches F1 0.889 on demo1, Llama/Llama/Llama reaches 0.947 on Ikea, and both reach 0.667 on Netonnet. The authors reject H1 that mixed models outperform on a specific site.

Across sites, Llama3.1/Mistral-Nemo/Mistral-Nemo has the highest average F1 at 0.703, versus 0.660 for homogeneous Gemma2 and 0.654 in Table II for homogeneous Llama3.1. The paper later prints 0.653 for Llama3.1; either way the gain is modest.

Median workload rises with site complexity: 15.0 steps on demo1 and 17.5 on demo2 versus 20.0 on Ikea and 25.0 on Netonnet; the paper gives an example of about 15 minutes on demo1 versus 56 minutes on Netonnet.

A random-forest classifier distinguishes which model produced first-step scene descriptions at over 94% accuracy, led by average length (0.27), noun-to-verb ratio (0.22), and adjective count (0.21). This establishes output-style differences, not that style mismatch causes coordination failures.
The authors propose mutual intelligibility, prompt fit, and site-complexity fit as explanations. They explicitly state that causality cannot be determined from the experiment.

limitations: Homogeneous versus heterogeneous model assignment is not equivalent to single-agent versus multi-agent architecture.
The best cross-site heterogeneous F1 is only 0.043 above homogeneous Gemma2, without uncertainty analysis.
Demo2 has 12 tied top constellations at F1 1.0, so it does not uniquely support homogeneous specialization.
A fixed Gemma2 validator and prompts developed mainly with Gemma2 and Mistral-Nemo can favor particular constellations.
The manual outcome rubric and one-evaluator process leave reliability uncertain despite author discussion of ambiguous cases.
The experiment does not quantify token cost, energy, licensing, maintenance, or production failure behavior.

Improve scraping, direct source-data access, and dedicated inference infrastructure for speed and reliability.
Extend beyond one purchase task and four e-commerce sites.

Repeated runs and explicit step/time measures alongside task effectiveness.
A dedicated validation agent invoked periodically with bounded execution and JSON-repair retries.

records.title: Triangle: Empowering Incident Triage with Multi-Agent

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Strong production and ablation evidence for a role-specialized multi-agent incident-triage system, but weak direct evidence for multi-agent superiority over a matched single LLM agent. The closest causal contrast removes multi-agent negotiation while retaining the surrounding system; all full baselines are classical or deep-learning triage methods with different information sources.
evidence_notes.research_design: Triangle uses Analyzer, Decider, and team-specific Manager agents across semantic distillation, candidate generation, tool-based information enrichment, majority-vote negotiation, and up to five reassignment loops. Evaluation uses 15 months of resolved incidents from large cloud systems: 12 months build historical knowledge and the next 3 months test it. Production impact compares three months before and after deployment for six recently updated services. Offline comparisons use ContentBased, InvertedIndex, LGBM, MART, and DeepCT; nine services test robustness. Ablations remove semantic distillation, multi-agent negotiation, or team information enrichment. A separate public bug-triage evaluation uses 200 assembled cases and semi-manual profiles for 20 developers.

held_constant: Offline methods are evaluated with the same hop-accuracy definition and up to five assignment hops.
Parameters for Triangle and comparison methods are optimized by grid search.
Component ablations share the Triangle pipeline except for the removed mechanism; without negotiation, the Decider assigns directly from ranked candidates.
omitted_or_confounded: No contemporary single-agent or single-prompt LLM is run under the same incident inputs, model, prompts, tools, team documents, information-enrichment access, and hop budget.

DeepCT receives chronological human-enriched discussions while Triangle generates tool-derived enriched discussions, so the strongest baseline comparison changes both architecture and information acquisition.
The exact foundational LLM and its decoding configuration are not specified in the extracted full text.
The production analysis is a before-after comparison without a randomized or contemporaneous control and does not disclose incident counts.
Only resolved incidents are included, creating an outcome-conditioned sample.
The bug-triage transfer study semi-manually constructs team-function analogues, adding human preparation absent from the main automation claim.

headline_results.finding: Across six production services after deployment, reported triage accuracy is 92%, 82%, 96%, 64%, 96%, and 97%; before-after TTE reductions are 18%, 91%, 48%, 72%, 61%, and 67%. Team D's 64% accuracy is a negative result linked by manual inspection to sparse templated descriptions.

Triangle reaches hop-1 accuracy 54.7% and hop-5 accuracy 91.7%, versus DeepCT at 43.4% and 67.6%. Because DeepCT depends on human-enriched discussion while Triangle queries tools to create its own context, this is not an architecture-only comparison.

Removing multi-agent negotiation reduces hop-1/hop-5 accuracy to 42.8%/70.4%; removing information enrichment yields 49.6%/65.8%; removing semantic distillation yields 49.1%/86.1%; the full system yields 54.7%/91.7%. The negotiation ablation supports collaborative decision-making over direct ranking, while enrichment has the largest hop-5 effect.
On 200 MSR 2013 bug cases, Triangle reaches 63.2% accuracy versus DeepCT 52.1%, MART 53.8%, and LGBM 54.8%, after semi-manual developer-profile construction.

The authors attribute gains to specialized knowledge, negotiation, and active external-information collection. The ablations support all three components, but a matched single-agent-with-tools condition is required to isolate whether multiple agents, rather than structured retrieval and iteration, cause the gain.

limitations: No matched single-agent LLM baseline is included despite discussion of single-prompt prior work.
The production deployment is large in data volume (about 600 million logs and more than 20 TB daily), but the number and distribution of evaluated incidents are confidential.
Before-after TTE can be affected by concurrent process, staffing, workload, and service changes that are not controlled in the paper.
Data come from a leading technology company's cloud systems and may not represent other organizations.
Accuracy and TTE omit false-positive rate, recall, calibration, per-incident inference cost, safety of tool queries, and human override rates.
After five failed loops, assignment may involve humans, so the system is not unconditionally autonomous.

Add false-positive rate and recall to the evaluation.
Disclose or prospectively measure operational costs, override rates, failures, and drift where confidentiality permits.
Run a matched single-agent LLM with the same retrieval, tools, model, and iteration budget to isolate agent multiplicity.

Hybrid candidate generation from historical similarity and team-capability documents.

Human escalation after bounded autonomous attempts.

records.title: iRUC: Reducing Inter-Microservice Data Communication in Data-Intensive Systems via Unified Computation

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Supporting evidence for a specialized generation-checking pipeline and for combining LLM agents with deterministic verification. It is not evidence that a multi-agent system outperforms a matched single agent: the measured runtime gains are primarily attributable to GraphQL+ unified computation, not to agent multiplicity.
evidence_notes.research_design: The study uses nine open-source Java and Go microservice systems, grouped by service count and deployed on cloud infrastructure. Claude 4.5 Sonnet powers four generation roles (labeling, modularizing, packaging, and GraphQL+ generation), Gemini 2.5 Pro performs independent functionality checking, and a PEG parser performs syntax checking in an iterative repair loop. Generated models are checked with 606 functional tests. Runtime experiments vary request data from 0.5 MB to 6 MB and compare iRUC with a conventional microservice system, excessive-transfer removal, dynamic deployment, and serverless computing under sustained loads.
comparison_controls: Within each project, all approaches use the same RPC and serialization stack: REST/JSON for Java and gRPC/Protobuf for Go.

There is no single-agent GraphQL+ generation baseline, same-model multi-agent control, role ablation, or matched prompt/tool/call-budget comparison, so RQ1 establishes feasibility rather than a multi-agent advantage.
The performance baselines evaluate different runtime architectures. Their results cannot identify the causal contribution of the LLM pipeline, which runs before deployment.
The serverless baseline runs on Alibaba Function Compute while iRUC and most other infrastructure is described on Huawei Cloud, leaving a platform confound.
Agent-generation latency is reported per round, but token use, API cost, total end-to-end generation cost, and a manual or single-model construction baseline are missing.
headline_results: All 606 normal, boundary, and exceptional tests passed for the generated GraphQL+ documents. Functionality checking took at most four iterations and syntax checking at most three, with averages of 2.0 and 2.3 iterations.
Per-round LLM-agent time ranged from 157.0 to 365.7 seconds across projects; modularizing, packaging, and generating dominated latency, while PEG syntax checking averaged under 1 ms.

Across the runtime experiments, iRUC averaged 5.57x the throughput of excessive-transfer removal, 1.52x dynamic deployment, and 1.87x serverless computing; its latency was 7.7%, 40.7%, and 37.4% of those baselines, respectively.

The paper attributes those gains to central execution near databases and elimination of inter-service transfer. This is a systems-architecture result, not a controlled single-agent-versus-multi-agent result.

Production claim versus evidence: the systems were popular open-source projects deployed on public cloud to emulate realistic conditions; the paper does not report live production traffic, incidents, users, or operational longitudinal evidence.
limitations: Only Java and Go projects were tested, and the selected data-intensive GitHub projects may not generalize to other languages, workloads, or production architectures.
LLM response variability remains despite iterative tests; default API configurations were used and no repeated-run generation reliability distribution is reported.
Throughput and latency do not capture total system quality, maintainability, deployment effort, model-generation cost, or correctness beyond the authored tests.
Centralized cross-database access introduces a larger security boundary; authentication, authorization, and policy enforcement were explicitly outside scope.
Repeated runtime experiments are mentioned, but repetition counts, variance, and statistical tests are not reported in the extracted text.

Add authentication, authorization middleware, and unified policy enforcement for the database gateway.

Deterministic PEG parsing and type/reference checks after semantic LLM review.

records.title: Cross-Model Collaboration for Enhancing LLM-Based Code Generation

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Core comparative evidence. CMCS directly tests when heterogeneous collaboration adds value beyond single-model correction, same-model collaboration, and a naive two-model ensemble. Its strongest support is for difficult code-generation tasks where models have complementary failure sets and execution feedback can trigger selective handover.
evidence_notes.research_design: CMCS partitions tasks between two models, performs stateless execution-guided self-correction, and hands unresolved tasks to the peer model for a fresh generation and repair cycle. Experiments span eight Python, C++, and Java benchmarks, multiple 7B and 14B open models, and proprietary models. Decoding is greedy at temperature 0. The study includes direct, prompting, self-debugging, INTERVENOR, MapCoder, naive-ensemble, same-model, component-ablation, model-count, correction-round, partial-test, and resource-cost comparisons.
comparison_controls: All methods reimplemented in the authors' pipeline use the same problem descriptions, public tests, runtime sandbox, and nominal maximum of ten correction/refinement rounds.
Same-model CMCS controls separate heterogeneous model complementarity from merely duplicating a model; a naive ensemble separates collaborative repair from the union of independent attempts.

The full CMCS path can receive initial generations plus a fresh generation after handover in addition to correction rounds, so the number of model calls is not strictly equal to iterative baselines even when correction limits match.

records.title: MapCoder: Multi-Agent Code Generation for Competitive Problem Solving

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Core mechanism and ablation evidence for role-specialized, same-backbone code generation. MapCoder supports the value of staged retrieval, planning, coding, and debugging, especially on difficult programming tasks, but its comparison with direct prompting is not inference-budget matched.
evidence_notes.research_design: MapCoder uses four prompted roles over one selected backbone: self-retrieval generates analogous solved examples, planning produces and confidence-ranks candidate plans, coding implements the best plan, and debugging iterates against sample I/O before trying the next plan. It evaluates ChatGPT, GPT-4, Gemini Pro, and Mistral-7B on eight basic and competitive-programming benchmarks. HumanEval uses k=t=5; most others use k=t=3. Studies include prompt baselines, role removal, k/t variation, extra sample tests, language/difficulty slices, and call/token accounting.
comparison_controls: Direct and multi-role runs use the same underlying model within each reported block and the same task descriptions, but their prompts, test feedback, number of attempts, and context are intentionally different.
The main comparison is not compute matched: MapCoder averages 16.7 API calls and 21.25k tokens versus one call and 0.64k tokens for direct prompting.
Several baseline numbers are taken from prior papers rather than reproduced, and Self-collaboration is absent for the difficult benchmarks, reducing comparability.
MapCoder uses sample I/O for iterative debugging and, for MBPP variants, exposes one carefully removed test as sample I/O; direct and noniterative baselines do not receive equivalent feedback loops.
Role-removal ablations are informative, but they do not compare the full transcript and token budget with a single monolithic agent prompt.
headline_results: With GPT-4, MapCoder reached 93.9% HumanEval, 83.1% MBPP, 22.0% APPS, 45.3% xCodeEval, and 28.5% CodeContests Pass@1. Relative gains over direct prompting were largest on APPS and CodeContests.

On ChatGPT/HumanEval, the full pipeline scored 80.0%. Removing only debugging reduced it to 66.0%, removing only retrieval to 76.0%, and retaining debugging without retrieval or planning yielded 68.0%; debugging had the largest average ablation impact.

Increasing retrieved plans and debug attempts improved accuracy but with diminishing and sometimes flat returns; adding five HumanEval-ET sample tests improved HumanEval by only 1.5 percentage points.
The resource tradeoff is large: averaged across reported datasets/models, MapCoder used 16.7 calls and 21.25k tokens per problem versus one call and 0.64k tokens for direct prompting.

Failure analysis found persistent difficulty with harder combinatorics, constructive, number theory, divide-and-conquer, and dynamic-programming tasks because of problem misinterpretation and incorrect plans.
Production claim versus evidence: this is benchmark evidence for standalone programming problems, not repository-level or production SDLC evidence.
limitations: Performance gains are confounded with far greater inference, context, and execution-feedback budgets than direct prompting.

The approach generates many tokens and calls; it reports no monetary cost, energy, wall-clock latency table, or cost-normalized accuracy.

Generated code must be sandboxed; the paper does not evaluate malicious code, dependency risks, vulnerability rates, or production integration.

records.title: Multi-Agent Assisted Automatic Test Generation for Java JSON Libraries

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Core production-adjacent evidence for combining specialized generation, deterministic post-processing, and validation in automated testing. It demonstrates real maintainer-confirmed defects, but it does not provide a matched single-agent-versus-multi-agent comparison.
evidence_notes.research_design: JsonATG starts from 681 maintained historical bug-triggering tests in fastjson2. A DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B Rule Generator grounds mutation rules in JSON-P/JSON-B documentation; a configurable Test Programmer summarizes intent and mutates tests; deterministic Java post-processing repairs packaging/import/wrapping; and a GPT-4o Test Validator uses three independent classifications and majority vote. Coverage is compared with ChatTester and ChatUniTest on six core classes. Ablations test free versus agent-written mutation, intent summarization, programmer backbones, and validator classification. A $25 campaign submits generated failures to maintainers.
comparison_controls: For RQ1, JsonATG's Test Programmer and both baseline tools use GPT-3.5, receive the same 681 seed-test set, and generate three tests per seed; baseline repair is capped at three rounds.

Coverage is measured only for six selected fastjson classes; JsonATG wins four but loses on JSONArray and JSONObject.

headline_results: JsonATG achieved substantially higher instruction coverage on JSON, JSONPath, JSONReader, and JSONWriter, but ChatTester/ChatUniTest were higher on JSONArray and JSONObject.

records.title: Teamwork makes the dream work: LLMs-Based Agents for GitHub README.MD Summarization

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Comparative but weakly controlled evidence that a teacher-student prompt-optimization pipeline can outperform a one-shot LLM on software-document summarization. The design changes model mix, context filtering, and prompt training together, so it does not isolate specialization or agent count.
evidence_notes.research_design: Metagente has four roles: a GPT-4o-mini Extractor and Summarizer, plus GPT-4o Teacher and Prompt Creator roles used to optimize a reusable summarizer prompt during training. ROUGE-L feedback drives up to 15 iterations per training item; successful item-specific prompts are consolidated. From 925 README/About pairs, the study forms random training sets of 10 and 50 and a disjoint 865-item test set. It compares GitSum, LLaMA-2, a single GPT-4o, and Metagente using ROUGE-1/2/L and paired Wilcoxon tests.
comparison_controls: All systems use the same training and test partitions, and statistical tests compare paired outputs over the 865 test items.
The single-agent baseline is GPT-4o, whereas Metagente uses GPT-4o-mini for extraction/inference and GPT-4o for iterative training-time supervision; underlying model use is therefore not matched.

The single-agent prompt is not described as receiving the optimized final prompt or the Extractor's reduced context, so model count, preprocessing, prompt optimization, and training compute are confounded.
No component ablation removes the Extractor, Teacher, or Prompt Creator while preserving models and budgets.
Token use, API calls, latency, monetary cost, energy, and inference-versus-training cost are not reported despite efficiency claims.
headline_results: With 50 training examples, Metagente achieved average ROUGE-1/2/L of 0.522/0.363/0.486 versus 0.282/0.152/0.250 for single GPT-4o, gains of 85.11%, 138.82%, and 94.40%.
With 10 training examples, Metagente achieved 0.536/0.377/0.503 versus 0.297/0.151/0.256 for GPT-4o, reported gains of 80.47%, 149.67%, and 96.48%.
Paired Wilcoxon p-values against GPT-4o on the 865-item test set were 8.62e-89, 3.40e-72, and 4.91e-91 for ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L.

limitations: ROUGE overlap with repository About text does not establish factual correctness, coverage, readability, usefulness, or absence of hallucination.

records.title: Exploring Autonomous Agents: A Closer Look at Why They Fail When Completing Tasks

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Core limitations evidence. Rather than claiming superiority, the study maps where autonomous multi-agent frameworks fail and motivates feedback-aware planning, navigation, observability, and early stopping as prerequisites for reliable deployment.
evidence_notes.research_design: The authors curate 34 executable web-crawling, data-analysis, and file-operation tasks with human-verified exact outputs. TaskWeaver, MetaGPT, and AutoGen are each run with GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini in isolated Python 3.10.14 containers using a general prompt template, yielding 204 runs and 104 failures. Three authors with at least two years of programming experience inspect complete traces and reach consensus on a three-tier, 19-cause taxonomy covering planning, execution, and response generation.
comparison_controls: The same task prompt template, task set, model versions, Linux environment, containers, and exact-match evaluator are used across frameworks.
Frameworks differ in agents, prompts, tools, memory, topology, and collaboration policies, so cross-framework scores do not isolate one mechanism.
There is no single-agent baseline, no matched call/token budget, and no component ablation of planning, coding, execution, or communication.
Only one aggregate result per framework/model condition is reported; repeated stochastic runs, confidence intervals, token use, latency, and monetary cost are missing.
Tasks were selected to be at least partially solvable and exact-matchable, which excludes harder and less easily automated real-world work and may bias success upward.
headline_results: With GPT-4o, overall success was 50.00% for TaskWeaver, 47.06% for MetaGPT, and 38.24% for AutoGen. With GPT-4o-mini it was 58.82%, 50.00%, and 50.00%, respectively.

GPT-4o sometimes underperformed GPT-4o-mini because extra planning conflicted with safety constraints or requested unnecessary confirmation, illustrating that stronger models do not monotonically improve agent-system reliability.

The taxonomy was consensus-coded without reported independent agreement statistics, frequency counts per cause, or external replication.
Framework versions and model snapshots are fixed, so results can age quickly as implementations and APIs change.

records.title: ChatDev: Communicative Agents for Software Development

evidence_notes.hypothesis_role: Core comparative evidence for role-specialized, communicative software generation. ChatDev holds the GPT-3.5 backbone and reported hyperparameters constant across a single-agent baseline and two multi-agent systems, and its ablations identify roles, review/testing phases, and communicative dehallucination as contributors. The evidence remains prototype-level and is not compute matched.
evidence_notes.research_design: ChatDev maps five subtasks across design, coding, code completion, code review, and system testing to paired instructor/assistant roles such as CEO, CTO, programmer, reviewer, and tester. A chain topology passes only subtask solutions as long-term memory while retaining within-phase dialogue as short-term memory. Agents seek clarifying detail through communicative dehallucination and use Python execution feedback. On 1,200 human-refined synthetic software requirements, ChatDev is compared with single-agent GPT-Engineer and multi-agent MetaGPT using GPT-3.5 at temperature 0.2, automated completeness/executability/embedding-consistency metrics, pairwise GPT-4 and human preference, component ablations, dialogue analysis, and time/token measurements.
comparison_controls: The paper states that all baselines share the same GPT-3.5 hyperparameters and settings and receive the same requirement tasks.
The comparison is not token-, time-, call-, or tool-budget matched: ChatDev uses multi-turn Python feedback and 22,949 tokens over 148.2 seconds versus GPT-Engineer's 7,183 tokens over 15.6 seconds.
Prompts necessarily differ by architecture, and the extracted text does not establish identical accessible tools or maximum inference budgets for GPT-Engineer and MetaGPT.

Ablations remove roles, communicative dehallucination, or later phases while preserving ChatDev's general pipeline, providing useful mechanism evidence but no full single-agent controller with equal interactions.
The multiplicative Quality metric combines three proxies and can magnify executability differences; semantic embedding similarity and code volume are not functional requirement tests.
headline_results: ChatDev scored 0.5600 completeness, 0.8800 executability, 0.8021 consistency, and 0.3953 composite quality, versus GPT-Engineer's 0.5022, 0.3583, 0.7887, and 0.1419.
Against MetaGPT, ChatDev improved executability from 0.4145 to 0.8800 and quality from 0.1523 to 0.3953 while using fewer tokens (22,949 versus 29,279) and similar time (148.2 versus 154.0 seconds).

records.title: A Pair Programming Framework for Code Generation via Multi-Plan Exploration and Feedback-Driven Refinement

evidence_notes.research_design: PairCoder assigns reflection, diverse plan generation and selection, loop detection, and repair direction to a Navigator while a Driver implements, executes, and repairs code. Both roles use the same foundation model within a run. The evaluation uses GPT-3.5-turbo-0613 and DeepSeek-Coder-Instruct-33B on HumanEval, HumanEval+, MBPP, MBPP+, and CodeContest validation/test, with an additional GPT-4 comparison. The Navigator samples 15 plans at temperature 0.8, clusters them into three representatives with text-embedding-3-large and k-means++, and otherwise uses greedy decoding. Public tests drive at most 10 generation/repair iterations; hidden tests determine greedy pass@1. Component ablations remove multi-plan exploration or feedback-driven refinement, and a cost study logs GPT-3.5 API calls and input-plus-output tokens.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: For reproduced conditions, the foundation model, 16K context limit, problem descriptions, public tests, Python 3.9 execution environment, and maximum of 10 code generation/refinement attempts are held constant. A later comparison also permits direct, CoT, SCoT, Self-planning, and Self-repair up to 10 attempts. The comparison is not fully budget matched: PairCoder additionally samples and embeds plans, uses separate role prompts and historical memory, and consumes different actual calls and tokens. Some GPT-4 and multi-agent baseline values are borrowed from prior papers. No monolithic single-agent controller receives the same candidate plans, execution transcript, memory, and total inference budget.
headline_results: With GPT-3.5, PairCoder reaches 87.80% pass@1 on HumanEval and 15.15% on CodeContest-test, versus 67.68% and 6.06% for direct prompting. With DeepSeek-Coder it reaches 85.37% and 14.55%, versus 76.22% and 6.67%. The reported relative gains are largest on CodeContest, where initial plans fail more often.

Under the later common ceiling of 10 attempts, PairCoder still reaches 87.80%, 80.60%, and 15.15% on HumanEval, MBPP, and CodeContest-test, versus direct prompting at 75.61%, 72.80%, and 9.09%; equal attempt ceilings therefore do not erase the system-level advantage, although actual calls and tokens remain unequal.

Ablation supports both mechanisms. On GPT-3.5 CodeContest-test, full PairCoder scores 15.15%, versus 10.91% without multi-plan exploration and 9.69% without feedback-driven refinement. The paper reports larger relative component effects on CodeContest-test than HumanEval.

The gain costs more inference. On HumanEval, PairCoder averages 5.28 calls and 5.98 thousand tokens per problem versus 2.43 calls and 1.19 thousand tokens for repeated direct prompting. On CodeContest-test, the corresponding figures are 17.56 calls and 24.06 thousand tokens versus 8.73 and 9.79 thousand.

Reliability remains bounded by visible tests. PairCoder passes public versus private tests on 95.73% versus 87.80% of HumanEval tasks and 21.21% versus 15.15% of CodeContest-test tasks; CodeContest-test failures include 60.00% wrong answers, 16.36% runtime errors, and 8.48% time-limit errors.

The evidence covers isolated Python functions and competition problems, not repository-scale development, deployed services, maintainability, or production incidents. No security or generated-code sandbox evaluation is reported.
limitations: Role count is not isolated from plan sampling, embedding-based clustering, memory, execution feedback, and additional inference, so the study establishes a PairCoder system advantage rather than a pure two-agent causal effect.
Public-test availability and coverage directly constrain repair; passing sparse visible tests does not guarantee hidden-test correctness.

records.title: Multi-Role Consensus Through LLMs Discussions for Vulnerability Detection

evidence_notes.research_design: A tester agent first produces a binary vulnerability judgment and short rationale, then a developer agent receives it and the two exchange queries, deductions, and insights until consensus or a maximum depth of five rounds; the tester's latest judgment is final. Every agent and the single-role baseline use gpt-3.5-turbo-0125. Basic and chain-of-thought prompts are evaluated on C/C++ code segments for function-call, arithmetic-expression, array-usage, and pointer-usage vulnerabilities. Three 1,000-item groups vary vulnerable prevalence from 80% to 50% to 20%, and precision, recall, and F1 are reported.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: The single-role and multi-role conditions use the same GPT-3.5 model version, code dataset, vulnerability categories, and basic or CoT prompt family. The architecture comparison is not inference-budget matched: multi-role discussion allows up to five rounds of 120 tokens and consumes 484% more tokens. The paper does not provide an equal-token single-agent deliberation control, role or round ablations, repeated stochastic runs, decoding settings, confidence intervals, or significance tests.
headline_results: Averaged across dataset groups, vulnerability categories, and prompt variants, the paper reports multi-role relative increases of 13.48% in precision, 18.25% in recall, and 16.13% in F1 over the single-role approach.

The benefit is not independent of prevalence. The authors report more obvious recall and F1 improvement when vulnerable examples are more common; absolute multi-role F1 values are roughly 0.796-0.875 in the 80%-vulnerable group but only 0.344-0.380 in the 20%-vulnerable group.
An example attributes a corrected false positive to the developer pointing out that wcsncat and its size argument prevent the alleged buffer overflow, after which the tester changes its judgment.
The reported accuracy improvement requires a 484% increase in consumed tokens, and no latency or monetary-cost result is given.

This is a two-page preliminary classification study on code segments, not evidence of project-scale vulnerability discovery, confirmed defects, production deployment, or operational security improvement.
limitations: Only one model version, four vulnerability categories, and short C/C++ snippets are tested.
The large token-budget mismatch prevents attributing the result solely to distinct roles rather than added deliberation.
Results vary strongly with class balance, and low absolute precision/F1 in the mostly non-vulnerable group implies substantial false-positive review burden.
No repeated-run reliability, decoding parameters, inferential statistics, calibration, adversarial evaluation, or production study is reported.
The tester remains the final authority even when maximum depth is reached, and the paper does not measure unresolved disagreement or harmful persuasion between roles.
future_work: Integrate in-context learning examples to guide the agents toward better collaboration during discussion.
combinable_methods: Independent tester judgment before exposing it to a developer perspective.
Bounded developer-tester dialogue with a consensus or depth-based stopping condition.

records.title: Large Language Model-Powered Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection: New Perspectives

evidence_notes.research_design: GPTLens separates open-ended smart-contract auditing into high-temperature candidate generation by one or two GPT-4 Auditor instances and low-temperature discrimination by a GPT-4 Critic that scores correctness, severity, and profitability. Thirteen Etherscan contracts with CVE-reported vulnerabilities are tested in six configurations: a one-output Auditor baseline; one Auditor producing up to three candidates followed by random, Critic, or oracle selection; and two Auditors producing up to three candidates each followed by Critic or oracle selection. Auditors use temperature 0.7, the Critic temperature 0, and every configuration is run for three trials. A trial counts only when function, vulnerability, and reasoning align with the CVE report.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: All non-oracle configurations use GPT-4, the same 13 contracts, the same CVE labels, and top-1 evaluation. The interventions are not budget matched: the baseline generates one candidate, while GPTLens generates up to three or six and adds a separate Critic call. Oracle variants use ground truth and are upper bounds, not deployable baselines. The paper reports no token, latency, monetary-cost, equal-call single-agent, repeated-seed, significance, or component-prompt control.
headline_results: With one Auditor producing up to three candidates plus a Critic, the contract-level hit ratio rises from 38.5% for one-stage one-candidate auditing to 76.9%, and the trial-level ratio rises from 33.3% to 46.2%.
Adding a second Auditor raises the Critic-selected trial hit ratio from 46.2% to 59.0%, but contract coverage falls from 76.9% to 69.2%; additional agents therefore do not improve every metric.

Randomly selecting among three candidates lowers trial accuracy to 18.0% from the one-candidate baseline's 33.3%, while increasing contract coverage from 38.5% to 46.2%. Diversity broadens recall but worsens top-1 precision without effective discrimination.
The two-Auditor oracle reaches 74.4% trial hits versus 59.0% for the Critic, leaving a substantial ranking gap; three of 13 contracts have zero successful trials in every reported configuration.

The study uses real exploited contracts, but only offline CVE-label matching. It does not measure deployment, prevented losses, analyst workload, novel-vulnerability confirmation, or replacement of manual audit.
limitations: Thirteen contracts and three trials per setting provide preliminary evidence without uncertainty estimates or significance tests.
The apparent multi-role gain is confounded with extra stochastic samples and Critic inference; there is no equal-token or equal-call single-agent control.
The Critic is the same model family that generated the candidates and is not grounded in execution, static analysis, formal verification, or human adjudication during selection.
Known CVE reports are incomplete labels for any other valid findings, so potentially real but unexploited vulnerabilities can be counted as false positives under the task definition.
Token limits prevent testing larger candidate pools, scoring across batches can be inconsistent even at low temperature, and no runtime or cost measurements are supplied.

records.title: INTERVENOR: Prompting the Coding Ability of Large Language Models with the Interactive Chain of Repair

evidence_notes.research_design: INTERVENOR uses a Code Learner to generate or repair code and a Code Teacher to turn compiler or test failures into a natural-language Chain-of-Repair before the Learner tries again. Main agents use gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 at temperature 0.2, maximum length 512, zero-shot prompts, and at most five repair turns; additional pairings use CodeLlama-7B/13B. Evaluation covers HumanEval, MBPP, multilingual HumanEval-X, DS-1000, and the 4,463-example CodeError repair set. Studies compare published model baselines, no repair, direct error-message repair, Self-Refine, one- versus multi-turn CoR, Teacher/Learner model pairings, error types, and API calls per repair turn.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: The most informative prompt study builds all conditions on GPT-3.5 and uses the same task datasets; Table 10 reports two calls per INTERVENOR and Self-Refine turn, providing a close call-count control for planned repair versus self-reflection. However, the headline no-repair GPT-3.5 baseline receives fewer calls, most Table 2 baseline results are borrowed from other papers, and prompts and feedback differ by design. Tokens, latency, monetary cost, execution hardware, repeated runs, and an equal-transcript monolithic controller are not controlled.
headline_results: INTERVENOR reaches 75.6% and 69.8% pass@1 on HumanEval and MBPP versus 60.3% and 39.8% for unassisted GPT-3.5. Across the reported code-generation and translation tasks, the authors summarize gains over GPT-3.5 as about 18% and 4.3%, respectively.

In the all-GPT-3.5 prompt study, one-turn CoR averages 53.6 across five generation tasks plus CodeError, versus 51.4 for direct compiler messages and 50.2 for Self-Refine; multi-turn CoR averages 61.6. After three turns on the five generation datasets, CoR averages 66.7 versus 63.0 for Self-Refine and 62.9 for direct error messages.

Teacher capability matters. With a fixed GPT-3.5 Learner on HumanEval, no intervention scores 60.3, a CodeLlama-7B Teacher 65.2, CodeLlama-13B 66.5, and GPT-3.5 Teacher 69.5. The same ordering appears broadly across datasets.

On CodeError, one-turn CoR scores 15.9 versus 9.8 for direct error messages and 5.2 for Self-Refine; multi-turn CoR reaches 21.7. The paper attributes the gain to compiler-grounded diagnosis of assertion, name, syntax, type, and other errors.
Table 10 gives INTERVENOR and Self-Refine the same two calls per repair turn, while Self-Debug uses three and Self-Collaboration more than three; it reports no token, latency, or dollar comparison.
The work evaluates benchmark programs and collected buggy submissions, not repository maintenance or production operation, and it does not assess generated-code security or safe execution.
limitations: Effectiveness depends on the foundation model's ability to diagnose errors and follow repair instructions; weak Teachers and Learners reduce gains.
Compilers expose syntax/runtime errors, but logical-error repair depends on the availability, robustness, and coverage of tests.
The strongest absolute comparison gives INTERVENOR multiple repair calls while the no-repair baseline gets one generation; only Self-Refine is closely matched by calls per turn.

records.title: A Catalogue of Evaluation Metrics for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Frameworks in Software Engineering

evidence_notes.research_design: The paper uses a four-phase review workflow: exploratory review of software-engineering LLM multi-agent systems, targeted review of metric studies and documentation, citation snowballing from a prior literature review with selection based on relevance, reproducibility, and methodological clarity, and catalogue construction. Systems must generate or execute code, use multi-agent collaboration, and define applicable software-development metrics. The authors consolidate 26 existing and 12 proposed metrics into Outcome, Process, Product, and Framework categories, preserving original definitions where possible.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: This is a metric catalogue, not an empirical comparison, and it deliberately excludes single-agent systems; it therefore cannot establish a specialist multi-agent advantage. The reviewed frameworks use heterogeneous datasets, objectives, and self-defined measures. The paper provides inclusion criteria but no reproducible search strings, corpus counts, quality appraisal, inter-rater procedure, or validation of the 12 proposed metrics. Controlled cross-framework comparison is explicitly future work.
headline_results: The catalogue contains 38 metrics: outcome measures such as requirements met and pass@k; process measures such as duration, tokens, utterances, iterations, rework, and per-agent use; product measures such as errors, dead code, and messages per line; and framework measures for human involvement and ease of use.

The review finds equivalent concepts under different names and identically named metrics measuring different constructs, which can make isolated frameworks appear optimal and prevent direct comparison.

The 12 proposed metrics add K-executions to success, ease of use, Sounds Good, rework ratio, human clarification count/score, iteration count, time per iteration, tokens per agent, messages/LOC, dead code, and framework ease of use.

Traditional code-quality measures such as complexity, duplication, code smells, and test coverage were not identified in the reviewed framework evaluations; the authors recommend adding them as complementary Product measures.

The complete catalogue has no explicit metric for vulnerability rate, safety/security violations, fault tolerance, recovery, or stochastic run variance. Its listed cost metric operationalizes cost as total tokens, so production cost and reliability require additional measures.
The contribution is a maintained evaluation artifact and research agenda, not evidence that any architecture is production ready or better than a matched single agent.
limitations: Single-agent systems are excluded by design, so the catalogue cannot support a controlled single-versus-multi conclusion.
The 12 new metrics have not yet been systematically validated for relevance, construct validity, or cross-context applicability.
Framework discovery and metric reconstruction are insufficiently specified for full review reproducibility, and some measures were inferred from logs, appendices, or result tables.
Preserving original metric definitions exposes fragmentation but does not normalize units, formulas, datasets, budgets, or model/tool conditions.
Security, fault tolerance, nondeterministic stability, monetary cost, and operational incident measures remain absent from the catalogue.

Expand analysis to less-studied frameworks and refine the metrics into a standardized, reproducible, conceptually grounded methodology.
Maintain the open-source catalogue through versioning and community contributions.

records.title: Demystifying LLM-Based Software Engineering Agents: A Review of Capabilities, Benchmarks, and Failure Modes

evidence_notes.research_design: Structured critical review of more than 20 primary studies published from 2015 to 2025. It classifies six software-engineering-agent architectures and compares reported benchmark resolution rates, estimated per-issue costs, and a synthesized six-category failure taxonomy.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: This is a cross-study comparison, not a matched experiment. The performance table mixes systems, base models, years, and SWE-bench variants; cost values are published or estimated. A relatively close reported comparison is GPT-4o Agentless 1.0 versus GPT-4o SWE-search on SWE-bench Lite, but the review does not rerun either system under a shared harness. The Agentless model swap also demonstrates that model and architecture effects can be confounded.

The reported table gives Agentless 1.0 a 27.3% SWE-bench Lite resolution rate at about $0.34 per issue versus 23.0% at about $4.00 for GPT-4o SWE-search; the review therefore rejects architectural complexity as a reliable performance predictor.

Within Agentless, changing the reported base model from GPT-4o to Claude 3.5 Sonnet raises SWE-bench Lite resolution from 27.3% to 40.7%, which the authors use to argue that base-model quality is a major performance driver.
Reported costs range from $0.34 to more than $10 per issue among systems with similar resolution rates, making cost efficiency a first-class production constraint.
The review's bounded claim is task-dependent: adaptive agents may help on genuinely long-horizon work, whereas structured pipelines are favored for well-defined localization-and-repair tasks.
No surveyed architecture fully addresses hallucination, context overflow, test overfitting, over-engineering, inter-agent correlated errors, and security-boundary violations together.

This process mitigates hallucina tion due to redundant verification. However, it also has the downside of coordination overhead.

quotes.text: When multiple agents are instantiated from one and the same underlying LLM, their outputs will not differ too much. Such problems must be taken into account in any critical analysis of multi -agent systems. When many agents make the same mistake, we call it a correlated error. We think that debate will correct these. But it actually reinforces them.
quotes.use: Qualifies same-model debate and identifies correlated-error reinforcement.

quotes.text: Cost per resolved issue has become an important secondary metric in practice. The measured range between systems from $0.34 (Agentless) to $10+ (some multi -agent configura tions) differs by more than an order of magnitude for systems achieving similar resolution rates, a difference notably not highlighted in benchmark leaderboard presentations.
quotes.use: Documents the order-of-magnitude production-cost spread hidden by accuracy-only leaderboards.

quotes.text: The optimum degree of architectural complexity is probably task -dependent: complex agents can afford genuine advantages on long -horizon tasks requiring adaptive decision -making, while structured pipelines outperform for the well -defined localiz ation-and- repair tasks that constitute most current benchmarks.
quotes.use: Bounds when agentic complexity may be justified instead of treating it as universally beneficial.

records.title: Bridging Design and Implementation: A Study of Multi-Agent LLM Architectures for Automated Front-End Generation

evidence_notes.research_design: Controlled comparison of Supervisor tool-calling, Hierarchical, and deterministic Custom orchestration for a shared Builder-Validator-Fixer React pipeline. The study uses 75 user stories and paired Figma designs from four projects, six generator-judge model pairings drawn from GPT, Gemini, and Claude, and reports 450 experimental instances plus a manual audit of 180 judge ratings.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: Architectures receive the same datasets, standardized tools, specialized-agent sequence, prompts, token accounting, and model families. Generator and judge are always different models to reduce self-preference, and prompts and API versions are fixed. This isolates coordination strategy among three multi-agent implementations, but there is no direct single-agent generation baseline, so the study cannot establish that the multi-agent pipeline itself beats one agent.
headline_results: Architecture changes quality by only about 3-5 percentage points but changes generator token use substantially; the deterministic Custom workflow has the best reported cost-quality balance.

Custom averages 1.40 million generator tokens versus 2.47 million for Hierarchical and 3.10 million for Supervisor, while full functional coverage is 53.3%, 51.3%, and 49.5%, respectively, and full visual fidelity is 58.1%, 53.0%, and 56.8%.
Prompt/context duplication, not additional code generation, explains the architecture-level token difference; prompt tokens make up 60-70% of usage.
Judge agents average 5.9 times the generator token use and are the dominant evaluation cost, so validation can erase gains from cheaper generation.

Across all configurations, full functional coverage is 54.1% and full visual fidelity is 57.9%; counting partial matches raises them to 76.9% and 84.9%, but complex domain-specific interactions remain difficult.

A maximum of two validation-repair cycles, refusal retries, JSX cleanup, and file scaffolding repair many low-level failures without full regeneration; 42 of 144 GPT attempts recover after retry and 13 remain unrecovered.
Gemini-judge configurations suffer systematic visual-evaluation failures, demonstrating that the evaluation layer itself can be a production reliability fault.
limitations: There is no single-agent baseline; all compared conditions use the same specialized Builder-Validator-Fixer pipeline.
The dataset contains only four open-source Figma/React projects and 75 user stories, limiting generalization to proprietary, larger, or enterprise systems.
The study evaluates front-end React generation only and excludes backends, authentication, dynamic data binding, and more complex state management.

Categorical LLM-as-judge labels may miss fine-grained behavior and visual quality; manual agreement ranges from 0.55 to 0.90, and two Gemini-judge configurations produce no visual scores because of systematic evaluation failure.
Findings depend on specific checkpoints and prompts; the paper notes prompt sensitivity and possible behavior changes after model updates.
Even with partial matches, the authors state that production-grade quality still requires human refinement and better handling of complex interactions.
future_work: Evaluate the workflow on larger proprietary and full-stack applications with authentication, backend data, and complex stateful interactions.
Develop lower-cost evaluation workflows because judge inference dominates total token consumption.
Improve handling of non-standard and domain-specific interactions that produced the lowest functional and visual coverage.
Retain human refinement for production-grade acceptance and validate judge outputs against broader human review.
combinable_methods: Use a deterministic finite-state Build-Validate-Fix graph when task dependencies are known.
Separate visual scaffolding from behavioral enrichment and map stories to only the relevant components to constrain context.
Cap validation-repair loops to prevent oscillation and require programmatic checks for blank renders, missing files, and compilation errors.
Retry detected refusals under a fixed policy, then sanitize code fences, pre-code and post-code text, missing exports, paths, and project files with deterministic repair tools.
Use a different model for judgment than generation and manually audit a sample of judge decisions.
Track tokens separately for generators and judges so architecture and evaluation costs remain visible.

quotes.text: Each round of fixes is re-evaluated by the Val- idator, with a maximum of two validation–repair cycles to prevent oscillation and ensure stable convergence.
quotes.use: Provides a concrete bounded-loop stability mechanism.

quotes.text: The token efficiency differences arose from how much context each architecture needed to duplicate and re-read, not from differences in reasoning or generation complexity.
quotes.use: Identifies duplicated context as the cause of orchestration overhead.

quotes.text: Judges are the domi- nant cost drivers, consuming roughly 3.3× (Supervisor), 8.1× (Hi- erarchical), and 7.7× (Custom) more tokens than Generators (Ta- ble 3). Averaged across architectures, this is about 5.9× more overall.
quotes.use: Quantifies evaluation cost as the production bottleneck.

quotes.text: The Hierarchical architecture consumed 26–126% more tokens than the Custom architecture but achieved lower functional and visual accuracy (51.3% vs. 53.3%; 53.0% vs. 58.1%).
quotes.use: Shows that extra coordination hierarchy did not improve quality under the controlled architecture comparison.

quotes.text: These results indicate that most failures stem from low-level formatting inconsistencies rather than conceptual reasoning errors, and that lightweight recovery and cleanup methods effectively stabilize the generation pipeline.
quotes.use: Supports deterministic post-processing and retry as low-cost reliability measures.

records.title: Understanding Conversational Patterns in Multi-agent Programming: A Case Study on Fibonacci Game Development

evidence_notes.research_design: Exploratory controlled case study of two role-specialized agents, Designer and Programmer, on one open-ended Fibonacci-game task in C. Twelve pairings from seven open-source LLM families run under a deterministic Python controller with fixed minimal role prompts, temperature 0.5, cumulative history, a 10,000-iteration cap, and two repeated runs. Analysis combines thematic coding, BLEU/ROUGE, word counts, manual correctness checks, and GCC 11.4 compilation.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: The task, role prompts, controller, turn-taking, termination rules, token cap, and decoding temperature are held fixed across pairs, and every pair is run twice. Model identity, model size, reasoning specialization, and symmetric versus asymmetric pairing vary together; the 12 pairings are not a full factorial design. There is no single-agent baseline, and repeated-run details are not reported separately because the authors observed no substantial differences.
headline_results: Only DeepSeek-R1 paired with itself begins with a correct solution and sustains it to the end; three other pairs start correctly but diverge after 3, 21, or 69 iterations, and the remaining eight never reach the required solution.
No pair starts off-task and later discovers the correct answer, so prolonged conversation provides no observed recovery benefit in this task and can destroy an already correct result.

Strong role alignment or compilation success does not establish task correctness: Qwen3:Qwen3 and LLaMA 3.2:LLaMA 3.2 compile 100% of extracted C programs but never initiate the required correct solution.
The sole convergent DeepSeek-R1 pair exhibits semantic echoing and many no-code turns, showing that convergence, interaction quality, role separation, and compiler success are distinct dimensions.
Despite a C-only Programmer prompt, generated code is 61% C, 37.9% C++, and 1.1% Python, evidencing instruction and platform drift.
Pair compatibility and interaction dynamics matter more than model size or lexical overlap in this case study; reasoning-model participation alone does not ensure progress.
limitations: The study uses one open-ended Fibonacci-game task, so correctness and convergence depend on task-specific evaluation criteria and may not generalize to other tasks, prompts, or languages.
Only 12 selected open-source model pairings are tested; proprietary models, future versions, dynamic roles, and larger teams are outside scope.
BLEU and ROUGE measure lexical overlap and may not capture nuanced reasoning or non-literal correctness.
The experiment has no single-agent baseline and does not isolate model family, parameter count, reasoning design, or pair symmetry independently.
The very high 10,000-turn ceiling exposes stagnation but is unlike a cost-bounded production workflow; token cost and latency are not reported.
Compilation analysis considers only C snippets found in conversations and labels instruction-only turns as no code, so compilation rate is not equivalent to end-to-end success.
future_work: Replicate on more complex tasks, programming languages, model populations, prompts, and richer agent roles.
Add tool integration and study whether compiler feedback changes divergence and recovery behavior.
Disentangle whether DeepSeek-R1 convergence is caused by reasoning design or model scale.
Calibrate explicit convergence and termination policies using repetition, topic adherence, role stability, and correctness signals.
combinable_methods: Use deterministic turn-taking and preserve complete trace logs for role and topic analysis.
Validate candidate code with a compiler and behavioral tests rather than semantic alignment scores alone.
Stop or checkpoint immediately after verified correctness instead of allowing unconstrained post-solution dialogue.
Monitor repetition, topic drift, role reversal, language drift, and no-code turns as runtime health signals.
Trigger model switching, prompt revision, human intervention, or fallback execution when monitored traces stagnate.
Select agent pairs empirically for the target role and task rather than assuming heterogeneous or reasoning-model pairs are compatible.

quotes.text: Together, these findings suggest that simply allowing agents to interact is insufficient and a deeper empirical understand- ing of how coordination unfolds over time is necessary to build reliable autonomous SE systems.
quotes.use: Rejects unstructured interaction as a sufficient coordination mechanism.

quotes.text: Overall, these results indicate that interaction behavior in multi-agent LLM systems is strongly model-dependent and prone to episodic breakdowns that are not captured by mean-level statistics alone.
quotes.use: Supports pair-specific and trace-level reliability evaluation.

quotes.text: A good compilation success rate i.e., effectiveness could be accompanied with poor role alignment, again convergence can come along with a lot of semantic echoing.
quotes.use: Separates syntactic success, role quality, and correct convergence.

quotes.text: In other words, we observed no cases where agents began off-task and only later discovered the correct solution. This suggests that once a correct solution emerges, it tends to be preserved for a bounded number of iterations (≤ 69 in our study), while later recovery is unlikely.
quotes.use: Motivates early stopping after verified correctness and shows lack of late recovery.

quotes.text: In practice, monitoring the interaction trace can help detect early signs of failure, such as repetition, drift, or role instability before time and compute are wasted on unproductive exchanges.
quotes.use: Provides a production-oriented trace-monitoring method.
