records.title: An Empirical Study of Waterfall-style Multi-Agent Workflows for Class-Level Code Generation

evidence_notes.research_design: Ablation-based controlled experiment on 100 ClassEval Python class-generation tasks. Three model backends, GPT-4o-Mini, DeepSeek-Chat, and Claude-3.5-Haiku, each run a RawPrompt baseline and four role-specialized Waterfall configurations comprising Requirement, Design, Implementation, and Testing agents. The 1,500 generated samples are evaluated with class/function Pass@1, SonarQube issue density, runtime exceptions, and manual root-cause classification.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: Each model is compared against its own direct-prompt baseline on the same ClassEval tasks and official tests. The four workflow variants remove Requirement, Design, or Testing one at a time while retaining Implementation, which isolates stage contributions better than cross-system leaderboard comparisons. All models use temperature 0.8. Only one first sample is scored, minor syntax errors are manually corrected before rerunning tests, and generated tests make the Testing-stage treatment partly model-dependent.
headline_results: Role-specialized Waterfall processing is not uniformly better than one direct agent: full-workflow class Pass@1 falls from 0.35 to 0.21 for GPT-4o-Mini and from 0.46 to 0.32 for DeepSeek-Chat, while Claude-3.5-Haiku rises from 0.21 to 0.22.
Workflow effects are model-dependent; the Claude variant without Design reaches the best Claude class Pass@1 of 0.29, whereas RawPrompt remains best for the other two models.

Waterfall stages reduce missing-code and consistency issues and can improve maintainability, but generally increase reliability and adaptability issues and shift failures toward semantic logic, return contracts, and overrestrictive validation.
Runtime-error counts increase by 10-53% over RawPrompt across Waterfall configurations; ValueError, AssertionError, and TypeError dominate while some low-level errors decline.

Testing has the largest stage effect. Omitting it often produces the poorest correctness and highest error counts, but including it can add reasoning and validation faults; Requirement and Design show comparatively limited effects.
SonarQube reports no Security or Responsibility issues in any condition, so the experiment supplies no discriminating security result despite measuring those categories.
limitations: The evidence is limited to 100 Python ClassEval tasks and may not generalize to repositories, other languages, or full development projects.
Pass@1 scores only one temperature-0.8 sample, so stochastic variance may affect model and workflow differences.
Generated Testing-agent tests may not cover all behavior, and function-level Pass@1 can misrepresent classes with interdependent methods.
Manual failure classification is partly subjective, and the experiment manually repairs minor syntax punctuation before rerunning tests.
The study reports no token, latency, or monetary-cost comparison, so cleaner code cannot be assessed against orchestration expense.
No security defects are observed, but ClassEval is not described as a security or adversarial benchmark.
future_work: Build adaptive pipelines that select stages according to model and task rather than imposing the complete Waterfall workflow.
Add cross-stage consistency checks and prioritize benchmark specifications when generated stage artifacts conflict.
Define clearer contracts and report both functional correctness and maintainability or quality outcomes.
Improve failure diagnosis while reducing subjectivity in root-cause classification.
combinable_methods: Retain requirement clarification and test planning but make design and validation conditional rather than rigid.
Constrain validators to explicit requirements to avoid adding unsupported input restrictions.
Check method signatures, return types and formats, and edge cases at every handoff.
Use official behavioral tests alongside static maintainability and reliability measures.
Apply cross-stage consistency checks before implementation and cap Developer repair at a small fixed number of cycles.
Choose stage composition per model using ablation evidence instead of treating role decomposition as universally beneficial.

quotes.text: Waterfall-style, role-based agents can improve code structure and maintainability by encouraging clearer design and validation. But this extra structure often adds checks or con- straints not required by the specification, which can lower execution success andPass@1.
quotes.use: States the central quality-versus-correctness mechanism behind over-structured specialization.

quotes.text: Overall runtime errors increase by 10–53% under Waterfall workflows compared to RawPrompt.
quotes.use: Quantifies the reliability regression against the direct-prompt baseline.

quotes.text: Waterfall workflows reduce structural errors such asMissing Codebut increase reasoning and validation issues such asSemantic FailureandReturn Mismatch.
quotes.use: Shows that role decomposition changes rather than simply removes failure modes.

quotes.text: We isolated all failing classes from the 1,500 RQ2 sam- ples (100 ClassEval tasks×3 models×5 workflows) and manu- ally inspected each to determine the root cause.
quotes.use: Documents the scale and manual basis of the root-cause evidence.

quotes.text: We mainly use Pass@1 to measure functional correctness. Because it evaluates only the first generated solution, it can be affected by randomness and may not fully capture model ability.
quotes.use: Captures the primary conclusion-validity limit of the matched comparison.

records.title: Multi-LLM Persona Generation for Virtual Focus Groups in Software Engineering: A Controlled, Multi-domain Study of Emotional Requirements Elicitation

evidence_notes.research_design: Controlled mixed-method requirements-elicitation study across mental-health journaling, personal finance, and fitness. It compares one-shot single-model, iterative single-model, two-model, and three-model simulated focus groups with human focus groups and Emotional Goal Modeling. The main design includes 24 AI and six human sessions; primary-domain same-model controls add two seeds each. Twenty-four independent source-blinded raters evaluate requirements, with coded dialog mechanisms, equal-effort downsampling, mixed models, and pooled meta-analysis.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: C0 versus C1 isolates iteration; C1 versus C2/C3 adds model plurality while holding six personas, prompts, turn caps, and orchestration constant. C1-MV and C3-SM same-model controls in the primary domain partly separate multi-voice structure from provider capability. Creator models voice their own personas, session order is randomized, human-baseline order is counterbalanced, and requirement raters are blinded to source. The same-model controls have only two seeds and one domain, so provider and plurality effects remain partly confounded.
headline_results: Three-model plurality raises the pooled validated AI-only requirement share by 14.7 percentage points over the iterative single-model workflow, with a 95% confidence interval of 11.2 to 18.2 points.

Same-model controls estimate a 9.3-point difference-in-differences attributable to plurality structure rather than provider capability in the primary domain, although those controls are small and domain-specific.

Persona diversity, contradictions, productive-conflict density, empathy events, and conflict resolution all increase from C0 through C3; pooled productive-conflict density correlates with validated AI-only yield at Spearman rho 0.86.

C3 requirements are more innovative than EGM requirements, while EGM is clearer and more feasible and human focus groups better ground natural tone and social acceptability; no method dominates every quality dimension.

The supported use is early requirements divergence, not replacement of users: heterogeneous simulated voices broaden candidate requirements, structured EGM makes goals and trade-offs traceable, and human engagement validates context, trust, and acceptability.

C3 runs are capped at roughly 10^4 generated tokens and yield about 15-18 AI-only clusters with 8-10 validated, versus about 12-14 clusters and 4-5 validated for C1; monetary cost and downstream implementation success are not evaluated.
limitations: Same-model ablations use fewer seeds and only the primary domain, leaving residual confounding between plurality and provider capability.
Prompts, guardrails, and moderator challenge turns can shape disagreement and yield; provider drift and seed proxies limit exact reproducibility.
Validated share depends on human rating interpretation, relevance cutoffs, coding, embedding clusters, and cosine thresholds.
Only three consumer domains, six human participants per baseline/domain, and seven reflective interviews are studied, limiting transfer to other products, regulations, and organizations.
Provider/model diversity is not cultural diversity because training data and evaluation are predominantly English and Western.
Synthetic personas have no lived experience and must not replace affected users, especially for sensitive domains.
The study evaluates requirements novelty and perceived quality, not whether implementing those requirements improves software outcomes.
future_work: Test multilingual prompts, region-specific models, culturally diverse participants, and additional regulatory and product contexts.
Replicate same-model plurality controls with more seeds and across all domains.
Examine alternative prompts, moderation rules, validation thresholds, and clustering cutoffs.
Trace validated requirements through implementation and outcome evaluation rather than stopping at elicitation quality.
combinable_methods: Use heterogeneous models for divergent candidate generation, then EGM goal-to-requirement traces for structure and human focus groups for grounding.
Preserve creator-voice mapping so heterogeneous perspectives remain active during discussion.
Bound turns and tokens, detect role breaks, retry once, log prompts and model versions, and retain turn-to-requirement traceability.
Measure productive conflict and empathy rather than raw disagreement, and require conflict to produce a refined requirement within a bounded window.
Deduplicate candidates with embeddings followed by human adjudication and validate them with source-blinded independent raters.
Apply stereotype guardrails, privacy defaults, consent controls, transparency hooks, and human review before prioritizing sensitive requirements.

quotes.text: We do not claim that simulated focus groups replace affected users or human focus groups in sensitive domains. Instead, we position them as a fast, reproducible way to expand the space of candidate ERs early, which then must be vetted, contextualized, and prioritized with people.
quotes.use: Bounds the specialist simulation claim to augmentation rather than stakeholder replacement.

quotes.text: A random-effects meta-analysis pooled the C3– C1 difference at +14.7% (95% CI:[+11.2,+ 18.2]), confirming a robust plurality advantage (diamond in Fig. 5A).
quotes.use: Provides the pooled controlled effect of three-model versus iterative single-model elicitation.

quotes.text: At the session level, productive-conflict density strongly predicted the validated AI-only share.
quotes.use: Identifies productive rather than merely frequent disagreement as the proposed gain mechanism.

quotes.text: Plurality diverges and reframes familiar pains (e.g., guilt after lapses) into new design moves; EGM structures these moves via transparent goal→subgoal→requirement tracing, improving feasibility and clarity; human groups ground language, tone, and social accept- ability.
quotes.use: Defines the complementary diverge-structure-ground production workflow.

quotes.text: Provider plurality is not the same as cultural diversity: most models are trained on predominantly English and Western data, and our evaluation pool is limited; future work should incorporate multilingual prompts, region-specific models, and culturally diverse participants to test whether the same mechanisms hold.
quotes.use: Limits model heterogeneity as a proxy for real stakeholder diversity.

records.title: Bugs in Modern LLM Agent Frameworks: An Empirical Study

evidence_notes.research_design: Empirical taxonomy study of 998 GitHub issue reports from CrewAI and LangGraph between December 2023 and January 2026. From 2,773 collected open and closed issues, bug labels leave 1,010 and manual filtering leaves 998. Two annotators construct an initial taxonomy from 100 random issues and classify 15 root causes and seven symptoms across five lifecycle stages.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: The authors scrape all open and closed issues to reduce sampling bias, require a maintainer or contributor bug label, manually exclude non-bugs, and use two independent annotators with consensus. CrewAI supplies a role-based collaborative architecture and LangGraph a graph/state orchestration architecture. This is not an exposure-normalized framework comparison and includes no single-agent versus multi-agent performance control, execution reproduction, or matched task workload.
headline_results: API Misuse accounts for 32.97% and API Incompatibility for 22.34% of reports, jointly 55.3%, while Documentation Desync adds 7.52%; execution semantics and changing contracts dominate framework reliability.
The Self-Action stage contains the largest concentration and symptom diversity, especially scheduling, tool invocation, graph execution, and state flow.
Across all issues, Functional Error accounts for 78.26%, Crash for 10.02%, and Build Failure for 6.71%; many systems keep running while state, planning, or tool coordination behaves incorrectly.

In Mutual Interaction, API Misuse represents 37.74% and Streaming Instability 15.09% of stage bugs; 92.45% of that stage's symptoms are Functional Errors affecting delegation and shared-state consistency.

Framework faults can propagate upward into agent applications and the LLM software supply chain, causing incorrect execution, resource misuse, and security risk independently of model reasoning quality.
limitations: Only CrewAI and LangGraph are studied, so other orchestration, tool, memory, and deployment frameworks may have different failure distributions.
The corpus is restricted to GitHub reports carrying a bug label; unreported, security-sensitive, silently tolerated, and mislabeled defects may be absent.
Taxonomy labels infer primary root causes from issue text and comments; disagreements are resolved by consensus, but no inter-rater statistic is reported.

Counts are not normalized by framework users, versions, releases, agent executions, or lifecycle-stage exposure, so they are prevalence within the curated report corpus rather than operational failure rates.
The study does not reproduce failures or measure severity, repair time, exploitability, downstream task accuracy, token cost, or single-agent versus multi-agent differences.
Filtering excludes documentation requests and infrastructure issues that do not involve framework logic, narrowing the represented production surface.
future_work: Develop lifecycle-aware testing and analysis that detects execution-semantic bugs before deployment.
Study state consistency, coordination, and resource-management bugs in multi-agent and long-running workflows.
Standardize APIs, dependency management, and runtime monitoring to reduce recurring systemic faults.
Extend empirical analysis to more frameworks and connect issue taxonomies to executable reproductions and repair evaluation.
combinable_methods: Test initialization, perception, self-action, mutual interaction, and evolution as distinct lifecycle stages.
Add API contract and compatibility tests around scheduling, tool invocation, message serialization, streaming, and graph execution.
Keep documentation synchronized with lifecycle semantics and executable API examples.
Pin and test dependency combinations and validate runtime configuration before agent execution.
Instrument state transitions, tool calls, delegation, streaming, and memory persistence with runtime monitoring.
Exercise shared-state consistency, concurrency, execution isolation, and long-running memory in integration tests.

quotes.text: When bugs arise in LLM agent frameworks, they can propagate to upper-layer systems and amplify their impact, leading to incorrect execution, resource misuse, and security risks.
quotes.use: Establishes framework bugs as a production and software-supply-chain risk.

quotes.text: From 998 issue reports, we identify 15 root cause cate- gories, with ‘API Misuse’ (32.97%) and ‘API Incompatibility’ (22.34%) accounting for over 55% of all cases. Most root causes concentrate in the ‘Self-Action’ stage, indicating that mechanisms related to execution semantics are the primary source of framework bugs.
quotes.use: Quantifies the dominant framework root causes and lifecycle stage.

quotes.text: The ‘Mutual Interaction’ stage features coordination failures, including ‘API Misuse’ (accounting for 37.74% of this stage) and ‘Streaming Instability’ (accounting for 15.09% of this stage), which disrupt delegation logic and shared state consistency.
quotes.use: Directly identifies coordination and shared-state failure mechanisms.

quotes.text: Future work can explore lifecycle-aware testing and analysis meth- ods to detect execution-semantic bugs early. As agent ecosystems evolve, research should address state-consistency, coordination, and resource-management bugs in multi-agent and long-running workflows. Finally, integrating our insights into framework de- sign, including standardized APIs, dependency management, and runtime monitoring, may help reduce systemic failures.
quotes.use: Provides the paper's production-readiness methods and research agenda.

records.title: Rethinking software engineering for agentic ai systems

evidence_notes.research_design: Structured multivocal literature review of 23 recent peer-reviewed studies, preprints, expert surveys, and practitioner-oriented sources. The paper uses qualitative thematic synthesis across engineer-role evolution, verification, empirical productivity and maintainability, and education and professional practice, then proposes a four-competency transformation framework. The search is described as iterative and guided by relevance, conceptual clarity, and contribution; databases, search strings, screening counts, and source-quality appraisal are not reported.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: The paper performs no original matched single-agent versus specialist-multi-agent experiment. It synthesizes heterogeneous external studies whose tasks, models, prompts, tools, and process conditions differ. Two reported comparisons are informative but answer adjacent questions: a cited evaluation found identical success rates with a 53-fold cost difference and 917 versus 3 tool calls, and a two-phase study of 151 professional developers found a 30.7% median speed gain during AI-assisted development but no significant downstream completion-time or code-quality difference when other developers evolved the code without AI. Neither comparison isolates multi-agent specialization under matched conditions.
headline_results: The review's central conclusion is that abundant generation moves the bottleneck from code authorship to intent specification, semantic verification, orchestration, and accountable human judgment.

The surveyed literature does not support a universally optimal agent configuration; the paper argues that team composition and orchestration should vary with task characteristics, domain constraints, and quality requirements.

A representative evaluation summarized in the review reports that models with identical success rates differ by 53 times in cost and by 917 versus 3 tool calls, showing that outcome accuracy alone can conceal major orchestration inefficiency.

The cited 151-developer experiment reports a 30.7% median task-time reduction during AI-assisted construction, but no significant downstream completion-time or code-quality difference; the review therefore locates maintainability in the surrounding review, testing, and verification process rather than generation alone.

The review presents multi-agent cross-verification as a way to catch domain-specific blind spots, while also warning that coordination is difficult and that using LLMs as both generators and verifiers creates correlated-failure and trust-calibration risks.
No evidence synthesized by this paper establishes that specialist multi-agent systems outperform one agent when requirements, prompts, tools, models, and inference budgets are all held constant.
limitations: The multivocal review includes sources of variable rigor and does not report a reproducible search, selection, or quality-assessment protocol.
Agentic workflow and orchestration are emergent constructs without universally accepted definitions, creating construct-validity ambiguity.

The review is bounded by a rapidly changing time window and data-source set, and much of the cited empirical evidence comes from controlled or large industrial settings that may not generalize to smaller organizations.
The proposed competency and transformation framework is synthetic and conceptual; its practical effectiveness has not been validated longitudinally or in real deployments.
The paper does not provide an original matched agent-count comparison, repeated-run uncertainty, or a common cost and quality harness for the systems summarized in its representative table.
Cross-model verification is proposed, but the paper acknowledges the recursive trust problem created when probabilistic models generate and verify the same artifacts.
future_work: Develop open standards for prompt provenance, prompt and specification versioning, and agent capability declarations.
Run controlled industrial experiments comparing orchestration-centered and authorship-centered workflows.
Integrate probabilistic LLM reasoning formally with symbolic verification methods and evaluate scalable hybrid guarantees.
Create end-to-end benchmarks for reliability under iteration, security robustness, and lifecycle maintainability rather than isolated generation accuracy.
Conduct longitudinal studies of workforce skill evolution, curriculum interventions, production team dynamics, shared understanding, and skill atrophy.
Develop mechanisms for auditability, liability attribution, and compliance in AI-mediated development ecosystems.
combinable_methods: Use human-authored domain models, business rules, constraints, and quality attributes as versioned ground truth for specification-driven agent execution.
Combine static analysis, dynamic testing, formal methods, runtime monitoring, and human review as layered assurance rather than relying on an LLM verifier alone.
Use independent models for cross-checking where appropriate and govern correlated failures with explicit trust calibration and final human accountability.
Select and compose agents adaptively by task complexity, domain constraints, capability, and quality requirements instead of fixing one workflow globally.
Maintain provenance for generated code, prompts, specifications, decision rationale, agent interactions, and trade-offs in audit-ready logs.
Place explicit human gates at architecture sign-off, security validation, and production deployment.

quotes.text: The consensus across these reviews is substantive: standalone LLM outputs cannot be trusted in isolation for produc- tion use.
quotes.use: States the review's production-readiness premise.

quotes.text: Phase 1 replicates prior findings: AI assistance yielded a 30.7% median reduction in task completion time. However, Phase 2—in which different developers evolved the resulting code without AI assistance—revealed no significant differences in completion time or code quality compared to a control group.
quotes.use: Separates immediate productivity from downstream maintainability under the cited controlled study.

quotes.text: Models with identical success rates exhibited 53×cost differences and vastly different tool-call volumes (917 vs. 3), exposing critical inefficien- cies in LLM tool use.
quotes.use: Quantifies why production comparisons must include tool use and cost, not success alone.

quotes.text: The evidence that no sin- gle agent configuration is universally optimal [7] implies that orchestration itself must be adaptive, with engineers selecting and composing agent teams based on task characteristics, domain constraints, and quality requirements.
quotes.use: Bounds the case for specialization to task-appropriate agent composition.

quotes.text: Provenance tracking, prompt and specification versioning, and audit-ready workflows should be treated as foundational infrastructure.
quotes.use: Identifies concrete governance infrastructure for production adoption.

records.title: AgentNet: Decentralized Evolutionary Coordination for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems

evidence_notes.research_design: Benchmark evaluation of AgentNet on MATH, BBH, and API-Bank using DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o-mini, and Qwen-turbo backbones. The reported test sets contain 140 MATH, 100 BBH, and 100 API-Bank problems, with separate training sets used for trajectory evolution. AgentNet is compared with five single-agent methods and four multi-agent systems; all multi-agent methods use three agents. Additional BBH studies vary three versus five agents, model and skill heterogeneity, router behavior, the evolution phase, agent count from three to nine, and executor-pool limits. Inference uses temperature 0.0, a 2,048-token maximum, and top-p 1.0.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: Within each table block, methods share a backbone and benchmark, and all multi-agent methods use three agents. The heterogeneity experiment crosses homogeneous, model-heterogeneous, skill-heterogeneous, and jointly heterogeneous teams at sizes three and five. The evolution ablation compares three-agent AgentNet with and without evolution on GPT-4o-mini. However, single-agent methods intentionally differ in prompting, memory, self-consistency, refinement, and likely invocation count; exact prompts, tool budgets, token budgets, and execution costs are not reported. AgentNet also bundles decentralization, routing, RAG memory, topology evolution, and specialization, so its single-agent advantage cannot be attributed to specialization alone.
headline_results: Against the strongest listed single-agent result per task, AgentNet scores 92.86% versus 89.28% on MATH, 94% versus 92% on BBH, and 30% versus 29% on API-Bank with DeepSeek-V3; 85% versus 77.14%, 86% versus 85%, and 29% versus 24% with GPT-4o-mini; and 81.43% versus 76.43%, 92% versus 74%, and 32% versus 28% with Qwen-turbo.

Scaling from three agents and 30 executors to nine agents and 40 executors raises training performance only from 80.38 to 81.18, while test performance fluctuates between 80 and 86; the paper explicitly describes diminishing returns.

The routing design updates task state only after execution or splitting, leaves state unchanged during forwarding, uses a DAG to avoid forwarding loops, and forwards completed subtask results without decomposition reasoning to limit propagation of one agent's decomposition errors.
The paper reports no token, latency, monetary, communication, or energy cost, and its privacy and fault-tolerance claims are not accompanied by privacy leakage or injected-failure measurements.
limitations: The evaluation uses mathematics, logical question answering, and API calling rather than repository-level software development, so transfer to production software tasks is untested.

evidence_notes.research_design: Architecture paper describing an implemented Test Generation, Execution and Analysis, and Review and Optimization loop on Python, Node.js, LangChain, Kubernetes, RabbitMQ, Dockerized pytest and JUnit runners, Git, FAISS, and PostgreSQL. The evaluation is reported inconsistently as eight modules in one table, eight open-source repositories plus two internal applications in the prose, and six projects in the dataset table. Projects are standardized to about 4,000 lines per module. Results are said to be normalized over three runs and compare static one-pass tests with an agentic loop capped at eight iterations.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: The baseline uses one-pass GPT-4o-mini test generation without feedback and manual pytest or JUnit execution. The treatment adds three specialized roles, GPT-4o-mini and Codex derivatives for generation, deterministic execution and coverage tools, AutoGen-style review, persistent vector and artifact memory, and up to eight refinement iterations. Exact prompts, model versions, call budgets, random seeds, and statistical tests are not given. Models, tools, memory, and inference opportunities are therefore not matched, so the reported gains evaluate the complete feedback pipeline rather than the effect of multiple specialist agents alone.
headline_results: The main quantitative table reports statement coverage rising from 72.8% to 94.9%, branch coverage from 61.5% to 91.7%, valid executable tests from 64.1% to 89.3%, per-module runtime falling from 3.5 to 1.1 hours, and QA effort falling from 11.8 to 3.4 person-hours.
The loop is reported to converge in 5.2 iterations on average, typically four to six iterations for Python and five to seven for Java, but the paper gives no variance or per-project values.

The conclusion gives still different improvements of 27% coverage, 42% execution time, 33% post-deployment defect density, and 38% manual QA effort; post-deployment defect density is not defined or tabulated in the methods or results.

Persistent vector memory is qualitatively credited with preventing prior failure contexts from recurring, and minor code-drift trials are said to trigger affected-test regeneration without retraining, but neither observation has a numeric control.

The paper cites external findings that synchronization degrades beyond four concurrent reasoning agents and that repeated LLM calls can multiply emissions three to five times; these are not measured ATA results.

Reported coverage, runtime, manual-effort, and conclusion-level improvements differ across sections without reconciliation.

records.title: A Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Automated Software Testing

evidence_notes.research_design: Controlled ablation on all 40 Python programs in QuixBugs at commit f2a4e2f, each with a seeded single-line defect and corrected reference implementation. GLM-4-Flash version glm-4-flash-250414 is used at temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.9 with a three-iteration cap. Every condition runs with five distinct seeds. The study reports unconditional, two-run differential, strict, and defect-line-attributable detection; execution success; tokens; latency; rounds; test-artifact categories; and defect-class distributions. Tests run in a Python 3.12.3 subprocess sandbox with a 30-second timeout and no network.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: The full framework, combined-role single agent, three-agent condition without diagnosis, execution-only rule, and diagnosis-only rule use the same 40 programs, model, five seeds, and iteration bound. The full system has requirement, generation, and diagnosis LLM calls plus a rule-based executor; the single agent uses one prompt for analysis, generation, and judgment. The execution environment and criteria are shared, but prompts and call structure differ and token use is not matched: 9,348 tokens for the full framework versus 3,120 for one agent. This is the closest controlled specialization comparison in the batch, but it combines role decomposition with about three times the inference tokens.
headline_results: The full framework scores 90.0% unconditional, 55.0% differential, and 5.0% strict detection versus 72.5%, 37.5%, and 2.5% for the same-model combined-role single agent; the differential advantage is 17.5 percentage points.

Removing the diagnostic agent yields 85.0% unconditional, 52.5% differential, and 5.0% strict detection. The 2.5-point differential loss is smaller than the full framework's reported seed-to-seed standard deviation, so the paper does not establish that the fourth role is necessary.

Execution-only detection matches the full framework at 55.0% differential and 5.0% strict detection, while diagnosis-only falls to 27.5% and 2.5%; the composite diagnostic term adds only unconditional detections that do not survive differential validation.
Every successful detection occurs in the first iteration in all five runs, so the implemented feedback loop contributes no additional detections on QuixBugs.

The full framework averages 9,348 tokens, $0.0056, 142.9 seconds, and 1.20 rounds per program. The three-agent condition costs 7,265 tokens and one agent 3,120; removing one role cuts tokens 22.3%, and using one agent cuts them 66.6%.

The nominal 90.0% rate falls to 55.0% under differential execution, 47.5% when a failing test must also cover the seeded defect line, and 5.0% when the suite must pass entirely on the correct implementation.
Thirty-eight of 40 generated suites fail at least once on correct code. Hallucinated oracle values account for 42.1% and API or signature mismatches 28.9% of these suites, jointly 71.0%.

Twenty-seven of 40 suites require AST post-processing to remove target-function redefinitions, including four manually resolved cases; four fully undetected programs require structural inputs not synthesized within three rounds.
limitations: QuixBugs contains only 40 moderate-size classical algorithms with single-line defects and does not represent module interaction, concurrency, industrial specifications, or repository context.
All controlled conditions use one base model, so the result does not establish whether stronger or different models retain the role-decomposition advantage.
The full and single-agent conditions share model, seeds, and iteration cap but not prompt structure, model-call count, token use, or monetary and latency budget.
Wilson intervals span roughly 30 percentage points at this sample size, and class sizes of one to six do not support comparative claims across defect classes.
AST post-processing changes 27 suites and requires manual resolution for four, limiting end-to-end autonomy and introducing an additional deterministic repair component.
Coverage of the annotated defect line does not prove that the assertion failure is semantically caused by that defect, so 19 attributable cases remain an upper bound.
No human evaluation measures test readability or maintainability, and no unified harness comparison with other agentic or search-based systems is run.

The reported cost is a lower bound for small functions; industrial context scaling is unmeasured, and live CI normally lacks the corrected reference implementation required by the differential protocol.

records.title: Towards Role-Based Multi-Agent LLM Systems for Software Requirements Analysis

evidence_notes.research_design: Structured overview plus a theoretical, exploratory architecture for requirements analysis. Four SWEBOK analysis activities are mapped to roles; paired task-specialized small language models produce reports in parallel, a distance threshold accepts agreement, and a supervisory large model arbitrates disagreement using output-uncertainty estimates. A simplified probability model multiplies step-success probabilities under independence. There is no implementation, requirements corpus, experiment, user study, or measured result.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: None. The paper does not instantiate a single-agent baseline or a multi-agent treatment and reports no matched requirements, prompts, tools, models, inference budgets, latency, cost, accuracy, consistency, or human judgments. Its equations illustrate a proposed mechanism and assumptions; they do not show that specialist agents outperform one agent.
headline_results: The proposed mechanism assigns each requirements-analysis role to two parallel specialized SLMs, accepts sufficiently similar reports, and sends disagreements to a higher-level LLM for contextual arbitration.

The paper explicitly states that agreement between the paired SLMs does not imply correctness; any redundancy benefit depends on the simplifying assumption that their correctness events are statistically independent.

For four stages with equal per-stage success probability P, the illustrative model gives total success P to the fourth power; at P = 0.5 this is 0.0625, which the authors use to show rapid cumulative reliability loss and the need for very high stage-level reliability.
The negative-decision case is not modeled, and neither the report distance, threshold, uncertainty estimates, nor arbitration reliability is operationalized or calibrated.
The paper offers no empirical evidence that LLM-SLM specialization, redundancy, or supervision improves requirements quality, stability, cost, or production readiness.
limitations: The contribution is explicitly theoretical and exploratory, with no implemented framework or empirical validation.
Statistical independence between paired-agent correctness and among requirements-analysis phases is assumed for tractability even though the paper notes that phases are not independent in practice.
Agreement can reflect shared error rather than correctness, but correlated model errors are not represented in the probability formulation.
The negative-decision and double-checking-failure case is not considered.
The vector representation, report-distance metric, similarity threshold, source and calibration of uncertainty, and comparison between LLM and SLM uncertainty are unspecified.
No compute, token, latency, or monetary cost is estimated despite citing high computational requirements as a multi-agent limitation.
SLMs are described as efficient and context-focused but limited in generalization and robustness; the architecture does not test whether supervision repairs those weaknesses.

Develop systematic measurements for uncertainty, hallucination, consistency, and error propagation.
Assess the limitations of the model and refine its independence, arbitration, threshold, and reliability assumptions.
combinable_methods: Map requirement artifacts to explicit SWEBOK-derived analytical roles with role-specific structured outputs.

evidence_notes.research_design: A 2026 MSc thesis presents SandBot as an implemented proof-of-concept and evaluates it on one described end-to-end task: designing, provisioning, deploying, testing, and hardening a three-tier web application through OpenNebula over approximately 40-60 reasoning turns. Additional simulations inject API rate limits, dropped or delayed VM requests, a 2,500-turn memory history, and five parallel 1,000-token-per-second streams. Prometheus metrics, Arize Phoenix traces, and JSONL audit logs provide telemetry, but the thesis does not report run counts, repeated seeds, uncertainty intervals, or statistical tests.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: The monolithic baseline is a single GPT-4o ReAct agent given the same MCP tools and Vector RAG as SandBot. The comparison does not hold the model stack or non-agent interventions constant: SandBot uses a GPT-4o Orchestrator plus Llama-3-70B and Mistral-Large specialists and also adds namespace isolation, Graphiti memory, compaction middleware, and Turn Efficiency heuristics. The reported result therefore compares complete systems, not specialist coordination against one agent under matched prompts, models, memory, and inference budget.
headline_results: For the described complex deployment, the thesis reports 94% total task-completion success for SandBot versus 42% for the monolithic baseline and attributes the difference to domain partitioning, isolated state, and a registry check that prevents completion while delegated work remains pending; the unreported number of runs and bundled interventions prevent a specialist-only causal conclusion.

The thesis explicitly warns that adding agents can hurt sequential workflows through communication overhead and information fragmentation, motivating strict separation of concerns rather than agent count alone.

Tool-schema deduplication is reported as reducing the tool section from 14,200 to 2,850 tokens per turn, while the paper repeatedly labels the reduction as approximately 47%; those two figures imply a reduction of about 80%, so the quantitative claim is internally inconsistent.

Tool-result compaction reportedly reduces OpenNebula status responses from more than 8,000 tokens to about 350 and prevents all observed potential ContextBudgetExceededError events by invoking secondary summarization, but event counts and summarization cost are not given.

Under simulated HTTP 429 events, the baseline reportedly fails immediately while SandBot buffers contexts and resumes all sessions; under dropped or delayed provisioning requests, its blocking timeout and explicit TIMEOUT observation reportedly preserve 100% provisioning success. The thesis provides no repetition counts for either percentage.

Production-readiness methods include immutable specialist configurations, bounded spawn depth, explicit prompt-section budgets, intent-filtered tools, turn-boundary delivery of cross-agent state, human approval before high-risk actions, MicroVM isolation, middleware cleanup in finally blocks, retry backoff, lifecycle reconciliation, tracing, and immutable audit logs.

The thesis claims hybrid local/cloud routing improves TCO, but reports no monetary cost, total token cost, or end-to-end latency comparison; it instead identifies inter-agent handoffs as a potentially prohibitive latency tax.
limitations: The system comparison bundles agent specialization with different models, persistent memory, prompt heuristics, and compaction, so it does not answer a matched architecture-only comparison.
Only one benchmark task is described, and trial counts, seeds, variance, confidence intervals, failure counts, and statistical significance are absent.
The reported 14,200-to-2,850 tool-token change conflicts with the stated 47% reduction.
Security evaluation simulates infrastructure delays and timeouts but does not report adversarial prompt-injection, VM-escape, privilege-escalation, or malicious-MCP tests.
The author identifies serialized handoff latency and a steep configuration-learning curve as adoption constraints.
Long-running Graphiti state can accumulate stale or conflicting facts and increasingly expensive graph traversals.
Keeping the agent's infrastructure model synchronized with external VM state adds substantial reconciliation complexity and strict asynchronous waits.

records.title: Code generation with large language models: a survey from neural program synthesis to autonomous software development

evidence_notes.research_design: A structured survey searches IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, Scopus, Google Scholar, and arXiv between January 2024 and June 2025, adds backward and forward citations, screens 513 records and 421 deduplicated records, assesses 132 full texts, and retains 48 primary studies. It synthesizes model architectures, code-generation tasks, prompting and retrieval methods, multi-agent systems, evaluation, security, deployment, and future directions; it performs no new single-agent versus multi-agent experiment.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: The survey reports that GeoColab's product-manager, algorithm-engineer, and programmer roles improve geospatial-code executability and accuracy by 7.59-26.09% over single-agent generation. This is secondary reporting from one cited study; the survey does not provide enough shared-model, prompt, tool, sampling, or inference-budget detail to establish a matched role-count effect. It also warns that model and benchmark figures are not directly comparable because of contamination, temperatures, sampling strategies, prompts, languages, and evaluation protocols.
headline_results: The strongest specialist-versus-single-agent statement in the survey is GeoColab's reported 7.59-26.09% improvement in geospatial-code executability and accuracy from product-manager, algorithm-engineer, and programmer roles; the survey explicitly says multi-agent effectiveness depends on specialization, communication, and coordination mechanisms.

SOEN-101 is described as emulating Waterfall, TDD, and Scrum with specialized roles, with Scrum reaching 75.2% HumanEval pass@1, but the survey supplies no single-agent value or matched control for that result.

Retrieval can ground generation in repository code and documentation, and execution feedback can guide backtracking or repair; however, retrieval precision degrades as repositories grow and current production-scale mechanisms remain inadequate.

Function-level benchmarks dominate because they are easy to automate, while repository-level dependencies, integration, evolving requirements, code-review load, merge conflicts, and cross-file consistency remain sparsely or almost entirely unevaluated.

Passing unit tests is insufficient: the survey reports that 30-32% of unit-test-passing solutions fail fundamental property tests and that generated code continues to exhibit API misuse and security vulnerabilities across models and prompting strategies.

Promising reliability methods include explicit preconditions and postconditions, execution-guided repair, retrieval, property testing, static analysis, independent security-focused co-decoding, formal verification, and mandatory human review for sensitive code.
The survey concludes that autonomous software engineering is still aspirational and current systems augment rather than replace developers.
limitations: Multi-agent performance is synthesized from cited studies rather than rerun under a common model, prompt, tool set, budget, or evaluation harness.
The 7.59-26.09% GeoColab result is domain-specific geospatial evidence and cannot establish a general software-development effect.
Benchmark contamination and incompatible protocols can inflate apparent progress and prevent clean cross-model or cross-method comparisons.
Most studies emphasize isolated, well-specified functions rather than large, evolving repositories with ambiguous requirements and collaborative workflows.
Pass@k omits security, maintainability, performance, integration behavior, and code-review burden; tests can also miss important properties and edge cases.
Repository retrieval loses precision as the relevant-to-irrelevant context ratio falls, and long-term architectural consistency remains difficult.
Security-focused prompts reduce but do not eliminate vulnerabilities, and automated static analysis has incomplete coverage and false positives.
future_work: Integrate neural generation with formal methods and verification-triggered repair to recover correctness guarantees.
Build contamination-aware, multi-faceted benchmarks for repository-scale correctness, security, performance, maintainability, and human collaboration.
Develop context management, hierarchical or sparse attention, retrieval, and long-horizon planning that operate at industrial-codebase scale.
Study human-AI divisions of labor, trust calibration, review workload, and long-term codebase effects.
Improve security-aware data curation, independent verification layers, and production evaluation on novel tasks and low-resource languages.
combinable_methods: Assign bounded software roles only where domain decomposition is meaningful, and evaluate the coordination protocol rather than agent count alone.
Retrieve repository code, API documentation, and usage examples before generation, with relevance checks at repository scale.
Express preconditions, postconditions, type contracts, and architectural constraints explicitly in generation prompts and handoffs.
Execute candidates against tests and properties, then feed structured failures into bounded repair or backtracking.
Combine static analysis, security-focused co-decoding, formal or symbolic validation, and human review for security-sensitive components.
Measure functional correctness together with security, maintainability, integration, latency, cost, and developer-review outcomes.

records.title: A Modular Multi-Agent {LLM} Architecture for Text-to-Diagram Generation and User-Guided Refinement

evidence_notes.research_design: The paper implements a text-to-diagram graph with a meta-selector, structural generator, deterministic renderer/validator, and optional refinement stage. Its quantitative evaluation runs the generator and validator on 20 easy and 10 complex prompts across a stated ten models, allowing at most three rendering attempts and recording final render success, first-attempt success, iterations, diagnostics, and latency. It states 300 runs, although Table 1 lists 11 model rows of 30 runs each.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: Every evaluated backend is wrapped in the same Agent 5 generation and Agent 7 deterministic-validation loop, so the experiment compares model behavior inside one pipeline. It contains no single-pass or single-agent baseline, no validator/remediation ablation, and no matched monolithic agent with the same prompts, tools, retry budget, and rendering feedback. Agent 3 selection and Agent 9 user refinement are described but are not part of the reported 300-run generator-validator experiment.
headline_results: The core handoff is explicit: selection yields diagram-type metadata, generation combines semantic intent with a formal grammar and style constraints, deterministic compilation returns structured diagnostics, and optional refinement makes feasibility-checked minimal edits before revalidation.

Across the same generate-validate loop, Table 1 reports final render success of 25-30 out of 30 per listed model and mean validation iterations of 1.03-1.37; these results establish renderability within the pipeline, not superiority to one agent.
The validator caps regeneration at three attempts, which bounds recursion and converts renderer errors into localized repair feedback rather than unconstrained conversation.

Most reported failures are syntax errors or an undifferentiated other category; missing-node, missing-edge, invalid-attribute, and style violations are uncommon. The evaluation does not include an independent semantic-fidelity score comparing source requirements with final diagrams.

Model differences are reported mainly in first-attempt stability and latency. Mean end-to-end latency ranges from 29.48 seconds to 613.12 seconds in Table 1, but token counts and monetary costs are not reported.

The easy/complex breakdown is explicitly preliminary, and several subgroup totals do not reconcile with Table 1; for example, glm-4.6 has 18 easy and zero complex successes implied by Table 2 but 25 overall successes in Table 1.
The paper's abstract says the architecture outperforms monolithic generation, but the reported experiment provides no monolithic condition from which to calculate that effect.
limitations: No single-agent, single-pass, or equal-feedback baseline isolates the value of role specialization.
Only the generator-validator subset of the four-stage architecture is quantitatively evaluated.
Rendering success primarily establishes syntax and formal renderability; semantic faithfulness, usefulness, visual quality, and user acceptance are not independently scored.
The study uses 30 prompts, only ten of them complex, and apparently one run per model-prompt pair, with no stochastic variance or inferential statistics.
The stated ten-model/300-run design conflicts with 11 model rows in Table 1, and multiple easy/complex subgroup values do not reconcile with the overall table.
Latency is measured, but token consumption, dollar cost, deployment reliability, and production user outcomes are absent.
future_work: Expand the diagram catalog and formal grammars.
Strengthen semantic grounding with domain-specific languages and graph-transformation back ends.
Add deeper human-in-the-loop refinement studies covering provenance, safety, and usability.
Explore multimodal inputs and visual question answering.
Broaden complex-specification benchmarks beyond entity-relationship diagrams and release prompts, logs, and metrics.
combinable_methods: Pass semantic intent and diagram type as structured metadata between selection and generation stages.
Ground generation in an explicit target-language grammar and separate global from diagram-local style constraints.
Compile artifacts with a deterministic engine and return structured diagnostics to the generator.
Cap validation-regeneration attempts and emit an explicit failure state when the budget is exhausted.
Check requested refinements for feasibility, apply minimal edits, and revalidate after each candidate update.
Keep CLI and GUI on one pipeline implementation so headless tests and interactive runs exercise the same control graph.

quotes.text: Each agent operates semi-autonomously within a shared state space, contributing a specialized capability (selection, generation, verification, refinement) to collectively ensure accuracy, coherence, and stylistic quality. This architecture embodies the principle of “reason–generate–validate–refine”, forming a closed feedback loop that mimics expert-level design iteration.
quotes.use: Defines the specialist stages, shared state, and closed-loop coordination design.

quotes.text: The rendering engine performs a deterministic compilation of the diagram code and produces diagnostic feedback in the form of logs or console messages. If the rendering process fails, Agent 7 encapsulates the extracted diagnostics into a structured feedback message and redirects it to Agent 5, requesting regeneration or localized correction. This establishes a closed validation loop that enables the system to autonomously refine the generated code until a formally valid output is produced. To maintain operational determinism and prevent infinite recursion, Agent 7 enforces a retry limit of three iterations.
quotes.use: Captures deterministic validation, structured feedback, and the bounded retry policy.

quotes.text: The refinement agent aims for minimal, surgical edits that satisfy the instructions while preserving syntactic validity; after each candidate update it re-runs the appropriate validator (Mermaid CLI, PlantUML, or the Markdown pipeline).
quotes.use: Shows how user-directed refinements are constrained and revalidated.

quotes.text: We evaluated ten large language models (LLMs) on 30 text inputs: 20 short easy prompts (easy001–easy020) and 10 structurally more demanding complex specifications. For each model–prompt pair, the multi-agent pipeline executed Agent 5 (diagram generator) fol- lowed by Agent 7 (deterministic validator).
quotes.use: Documents the actual evaluated stages and dataset size, exposing the absence of a monolithic condition.

quotes.text: Future work will extend the diagram catalog and grammars, strengthen semantic ground- ing through DSLs and graph-transformation back ends, and deepen human-in-the-loop refinement (provenance, safety, and usability studies).
quotes.use: Records the planned methods for semantic grounding and production-oriented human oversight.

records.title: MACV: A Specialized Multi-Agent and Consensus Framework for Reliable LLM Outputs

evidence_notes.research_design: MACV sends a GPT-3.5-turbo draft and GPT-4-turbo-extracted claims to a Tavily-backed fact checker, a domain validator using mock finance data or targeted science/medical searches, and an adversarial logic tester; static rules aggregate their verdicts. It compares a single GPT-3.5-turbo baseline, GPT-4-turbo RAG, GPT-4-turbo self-correction, and MACV variants on ten questions each from SQuAD, SciQ, and FinQA. GPT-4-turbo evaluates correctness against ground truth with manual hallucination spot-checks; processing time, tokens, and API cost are said to be tracked, but only time and qualitative cost effects are reported.
evidence_notes.comparison_controls: Dataset subsets are shared, but models, tools, and inference budgets are not matched: the single baseline uses GPT-3.5-turbo alone, whereas full MACV adds GPT-4-turbo claim extraction and verification, web search, domain sources, adversarial testing, and multiple calls. RAG and self-correction use GPT-4-turbo. The experiment therefore establishes a preliminary complete-system difference, not a pure causal effect of specialist roles under matched models, prompts, tools, or compute. It is a general/science/finance QA evaluation rather than a software-development task.
headline_results: Full MACV is reported at 72.7% accuracy versus 50.0% for the single-LLM baseline and at a 27.3% hallucination rate versus 50.0%, both described as 45% relative improvements; only ten items per dataset make these illustrative estimates.

RAG reaches 53.3% accuracy and self-correction 56.7%, while the full fact-checking, domain-validation, and adversarial stack reaches 72.7%; ablation discussion identifies fact-checking as the most important component.
The result costs approximately 23 times the baseline latency: 12.48 seconds versus 0.53 seconds. Higher API cost is acknowledged, but no token or monetary totals are reported.
The consensus produces zero reported false acceptances but rejects six correct responses, exposing a precision-favoring conservative bias that may suit high-stakes settings but lowers recall.
GPT-4-turbo claim extraction reaches 92% precision and 88% recall on 30 manually annotated responses; omitted or oversplit claims can propagate errors into all downstream validators.

A ten-question SciQ substitution reports that a less aligned Llama-X generator reduces MACV accuracy from 72.7% to 66.7% and raises hallucination from 27.3% to 33.3%, so verification mitigates but does not erase base-model quality differences.
The modular mechanism combines independently specialized evidence, domain, and logic checks, but the static equal-reliability consensus cannot account for per-agent or per-domain calibration.
limitations: The evaluation contains only ten items per dataset; the authors explicitly state that it is not statistically stable and that variant differences may not be significant.
Models, retrieval access, calls, prompts, and compute are unequal across the single-LLM, RAG, self-correction, and MACV systems.
The tasks are question answering rather than software requirements, coding, testing, repository maintenance, or deployment.
Correctness is judged automatically by GPT-4-turbo, with only manual spot-checks for hallucinations, and no independent blinded human evaluation is reported.
Static consensus assumes fixed equal reliability, while domain databases can be incomplete or outdated and web-search quality and recency vary.
Conservative rules reject correct answers, and noisy claim extraction can omit details before verification begins.
Horizontal scalability is an architectural claim only; full-dataset throughput has not been demonstrated.
The stated 30-item design does not make the reported 72.7% denominator transparent, and no confidence intervals are provided.
future_work: Learn per-agent and per-domain reliability weights with held-out calibration and probabilistic consensus instead of fixed rules.
Balance precision and recall to reduce rejection of correct outputs.
Integrate real-time knowledge sources and improve claim extraction.
Use adaptive verification policies to reduce latency and API cost.
Run larger-scale evaluations across complete and broader datasets before making scalability or real-world claims.
combinable_methods: Extract atomic claims before verification and retain extraction-quality measurements because upstream omissions propagate.
Run retrieval fact-checking, domain-rule validation, and adversarial logic checks independently and in parallel.
Return structured Supported, Refuted, Insufficient, Valid, Invalid, Inconclusive, Robust, and Weak verdicts with evidence and rationale.
Use explicit consensus rejection rules for high-stakes precision, while measuring false rejection and calibrating agent reliability by domain.
Checkpoint results and track per-model tokens, monetary cost, and wall-clock latency for every verification path.
Apply expensive multi-verifier consensus selectively according to risk, uncertainty, and latency budget rather than to every request.

quotes.text: Some models are great at fluent drafting, others at retrieval and factual grounding, and specialized validators can enforce domain specific constraints. By orchestrating these strengths and applying a consensus mechanism, MACV aims to reduce hallucinations while keeping latency and compute within practical limits.
quotes.use: States the heterogeneous-specialization rationale behind MACV.

quotes.text: This consensus policy treats all verification agents as having fixed, equal reliability and applies static rules; it does not adapt weights or thresholds based on observed past performance of individual agents.
quotes.use: Defines the consensus assumption that limits calibration and robustness.

quotes.text: These small sample sizes are sufficient to illustrate the behavior of the MACV pipeline but are not adequate for statistically stable benchmarking. All reported metrics should therefore be interpreted as preliminary and illustrative rather than definitive estimates of real-world performance.
quotes.use: Provides the authors' explicit bound on the comparative evidence.

quotes.text: Accuracy improvement: Full MSV achieved 72.7% accuracy compared to 50.0% for the single LLM baseline, representing a 45% relative improvement. – Hallucination reduction: The hallucination rate decreased from 50.0% (baseline) to 27.3% (Full MSV), a 45% relative reduction. – Processing overhead: Full MSV requires approximately 23× longer processing time than the baseline, highlighting the accuracy-latency trade-off.
quotes.use: Records the reported accuracy, hallucination, and latency trade-off together.

quotes.text: Future Work: Key directions include optimizing the consensus mechanism to better balance precision and recall, integrating real-time knowledge sources, implementing adaptive verification strategies to reduce costs, and conducting larger-scale evaluations to validate these findings across broader datasets.
quotes.use: Captures the proposed stability, cost, and validation extensions.
